entry.title: Commercial Overview — the home screen
entry.purpose: The one screen that shows the whole commercial desk at a glance: how many enquiries are still open, how many orders are live and what stage each is sitting at, how many stock holds are running and which are about to lapse, how many packed lists are waiting to be checked, and which orders cannot be dispatched because the advance has not come in. Nothing is created or changed here — every number is either a doorway into the list it counts or an explanation of how it was worked out, so the Overview is where you decide what to work on next.
entry.whoActs: Nobody writes on this screen — it is a reading screen for everyone, including Santosh. What changes from person to person is WHAT APPEARS. Unlike the rest of the module, a figure you are not entitled to is absent, not greyed out, because a greyed-out count of orders would still be a count you are not meant to see; the number is never even sent to your browser. Santosh (manager): sees everything on the screen except the two production-planning tiles, which belong to the one admin login. Setumani (executive): the same tiles as Santosh, with one difference — inside the "Waiting for an advance" explanation she is told to record the money, and not told she may waive it. Her enquiry count is there even though the enquiries screen behind it is read-only for her. Raghav (documents): no "Open enquiries" tile, no "Active holds" tile, no "Holds lapsing within 48 hours" card, and no "Waiting for an advance" tile. He sees open orders, the packing figure, the stage strip and the activity list. Murali (logistics): sees the enquiry count, the orders, the holds tile AND the lapsing-holds card (he can read stock but not change it), the packing figure and the advance tile — his "Awaiting dispatch check" tile opens Packing Lists rather than the Dispatch Check, and like Setumani he gets no waiver sentence. The bay 5 dispatch team has no Overview at all: the Commercial home is not one of their screens, and they work from the Dispatch Check row in their own sidebar. Only the one admin login sees "Production queue" and "Planned but not scheduled".
steps: Open Commercial from the sidebar — Overview is the first row. The heading reads "Commercial" with the line "Enquiries, internal sales orders, stock holds, proforma invoices, packing lists, the dispatch check, invoices and delivery challans." underneath.

Wait a moment while the figures arrive. Until they do, the whole body of the screen is a single dashed box saying "Loading…". The numbers are a snapshot of the instant the page loaded — there is no automatic refresh and no refresh button, so reload the page to get fresh ones.

Read the row of number tiles across the top. "Open enquiries" counts enquiries still New or Quoted — not yet turned into an order and not marked lost. "Open orders" counts every order except Closed and Cancelled, with the faint line beneath it saying how many exist in all. "Active holds" counts slabs reserved and not yet packed, released or lapsed, with a second line reading e.g. "3 lapse within 48h". "Awaiting dispatch check" counts packing lists that have been sent for checking and not yet checked. "Waiting for an advance" counts orders at Ready or Invoiced whose advance money is still short.

Click a tile that is a link to go to its list. "Open enquiries" opens the enquiries list. "Open orders" opens the orders board. "Awaiting dispatch check" opens the Dispatch Check for Santosh and Setumani, and the Packing Lists screen for Raghav and Murali — the same tile, two destinations, because those two have no dispatch check.

For the three tiles that do NOT respond to a click — "Active holds", "Planned but not scheduled" and "Waiting for an advance" — click the small grey circle marked "i" in the tile's top right corner instead. A little white panel opens explaining how the figure is worked out, and where there is somewhere to go, the link sits inside that panel ("Open production planning →", "Open the orders board →"). The tiles that are links carry no "i" circle at all, so a tile either clicks through or explains itself, never both.

Read "Orders by stage" below the tiles: eleven small boxes, Draft, Confirmed, Stock checked, PI issued, Packing, Dispatch check, Ready, Invoiced, Dispatched, Closed, Cancelled, each with its count. Click any one to open the orders board already filtered to that stage; the board then shows a line saying which stage it is showing, with "clear" beside it.

Read "Holds lapsing within 48 hours" on the left: each line shows the hold's reference, the customer, how many slabs, and the exact date and time it lapses. Click the reference to open that order's Stock tab, where Santosh or Setumani can extend or release the hold — Murali can open the same tab but only look. When there are none the card simply says "None."

Read "Latest activity" on the right: the last twelve things that happened on any order — the order number, a small tag naming what happened, the note, who did it and when. Click the order number to open the order. When nothing has happened yet the card says "Nothing yet."
Do the actual work on the screen you landed on. Nothing on the Overview can be edited, saved or acted on.
refusals: The bay 5 dispatch team cannot open this screen. If one of them follows an old link to the Commercial home they get a page headed "You do not have access to that page" with the line "Your login is not allowed to open /office/commercial." They are not quietly forwarded to the Dispatch Check, and they do not sign in here either — they sign in to their usual shop-floor start page and reach the Dispatch Check from the "Verification" heading in their own sidebar. The rule exists because bay 5's whole job is verifying packed slabs: they were deliberately given one screen and no reading of anyone else's work, so the desk's figures are not theirs to see.

A login with no commercial work of any kind gets the same page — "You do not have access to that page", "Your login is not allowed to open /office/commercial." The rule exists because the module asks one question before anything else — does this login do ANYTHING here — and echoing back the exact link that was refused is the difference between "I need access to that screen" and "the ERP keeps throwing me out".

Raghav gets no enquiry count, no holds figure, no lapsing-holds card and no advance tile — they are simply not on his screen, and the numbers behind them are never even sent to his browser. The rule exists because his part of this module is the invoice, the checklist and the challans; a hidden tile whose number still travelled to the browser would be a hidden number, not a refused one.

If the figures cannot be fetched, every number is replaced by one dashed box carrying the reason, and there is no "Try again" button — reload the page. If the session has lapsed the box reads "Not available for this login." or "Please sign in." The rule exists because a screen that silently shows nothing is indistinguishable from a screen that says there is nothing, so the refusal is stated where the figures would have been.

If the server is in trouble the same box names which kind of trouble, always with the number in it: "The server answered with nothing (HTTP 500). Something failed on the server, not in the browser.", or for a slow one "The server answered with nothing (HTTP 504). The request took too long — the server gave up before answering.", or "The server is not answering right now.", or, if you have been idle, "The server sent a web page instead of data (HTTP 200). If you were idle for a while, sign in again." Sometimes a crash reports itself and the box shows the server's own technical sentence instead — copy it as it stands when you report it. The catch-all wording is "Could not load the overview". These exist so the reader can tell a crash from a timeout from being signed out, and knows whether to reload, wait, or sign in again.

The "Waiting for an advance" panel explains the refusal that stops the truck: "Dispatch refuses these." Downstream, on the order itself, the wording is "The advance is short: ₹3,00,000 of the ₹9,00,000 asked (30% of ₹30,00,000)." or, when the order has not been priced, "The order has no total yet, so the 30% advance cannot be worked out: price the line items, or waive the advance." The rule exists because goods do not leave the yard before the agreed share of the money has arrived — and it is a figure, not a tick, so one token rupee no longer clears it.

The panel offers the waiver sentence — "or waive the advance there with a reason" — only to Santosh and the admin. Setumani and Murali see the identical tile with that half-sentence missing, because they can type the receipt in but cannot waive. On the order itself the refusal reads "Only the Commercial Manager or an admin may do that — or waive the advance on the receipts card, which asks for a reason in writing and is logged." and a blank reason is refused with "Give a reason for waiving the advance". The rule exists because letting a truck go without the money is a commercial decision the manager has to own in writing.
gotchas: Three tiles do not respond to a click and that is deliberate, not a broken link: "Active holds", "Planned but not scheduled" and "Waiting for an advance". There is no list of holds anywhere — a hold is only ever read on its own order's Stock tab — so the holds tile states itself and the card below carries the links that work. Use the small grey "i" circle on those three; the working links live inside that panel, because a link wrapped around the whole tile would swallow the click on the "i" and the explanation could never open.
The "i" panels mention "answer 11", "answer 12" and "answer 13". Those are numbered entries in the owner's list of decisions about how this module should behave, not anything you need to look up.
"Open orders" leaves out Closed and Cancelled. The faint line under it — "142 in all" — is the figure that includes them, so the two numbers are supposed to differ.
"Orders by stage" always prints all eleven stages, even the ones standing at zero. Clicking a zero opens a correctly empty orders board; nothing is wrong.
"n lapse within 48h" and the list below it both stop at twenty. If twenty-five holds really are lapsing, the tile will still say twenty — treat twenty as "twenty or more" and work the list down.

The holds figures are not re-checked against the yard when this screen loads. A hold whose time ran out overnight can still be counted as active and can sit in the lapsing list with a date and time already in the past; open it, or open the order's Stock tab, and it settles itself and reads as lapsed. So a past time on that list means "already gone", not "about to go".

A hold placed against an enquiry rather than against an order has no order to open, so clicking its reference lands you on the whole orders board. Those are old ones — a hold can only be placed on an order now. Read it as "this hold is not attached to an order", not as a fault.

"Awaiting dispatch check" counts only the lists sitting submitted and waiting. A list the checkers sent back drops off the count until packing sends it in again, so the tile can fall without anything being checked.

"Waiting for an advance" is not simply "no advance received". It counts an order as waiting when the advance money received in the ORDER's own currency is still short of the percentage the proforma asked for, and it also counts an order that has no total yet — because a percentage of nothing cannot be shown to have arrived. Advance money taken in a different currency counts towards it only if the exchange rate typed on that order's live invoice can convert it.

An order that asks for no advance at all (nought per cent) is settled and never in that count, and neither is one whose advance has been formally waived — even though a waiver puts no money on the order. They are off the list for good.

"Waiting for an advance" only examines the five hundred most recently created Ready and Invoiced orders. Comfortably above the real number today, but it is a headline figure on a dashboard and not an audit.

"Awaiting dispatch check" is one tile with two destinations. Santosh and Setumani go to the Dispatch Check; Raghav and Murali go to Packing Lists, because neither of them is allowed on the dispatch check. Do not assume a colleague sees the same screen when they click the same number.

The "Production queue" and "Planned but not scheduled" tiles belong to the one admin login only — not even Santosh sees them. The queue figure counts requests queued or scheduled, with a grey line for how many are running. "Planned but not scheduled" counts reductions made on the planning page that nobody has added back or removed, i.e. slabs an order asked for that the plant has not been told to make. Both lead out of the Commercial module into the separate Production Planning tab, which moved out of Commercial on 17 September 2026.

If you are still signed in on the old shared "Commercial" login rather than your own, you get Santosh's set of tiles but without the waiver sentence in the advance panel. That is the login, not a mistake — it disappears once everyone is on their own.
The numbers are frozen at the moment the page opened. Nothing ticks over on its own — reload the page before reading anything off it in a meeting.
"Latest activity" is the last twelve events across every order on the desk, not just yours, and not just today's. If the desk is busy it will not reach back very far.
entry.handsTo: The Overview hands nothing on by itself — it is the map, not a step in the chain. It hands the READER to the right screen: the enquiry count to Murali or Santosh on the Enquiries screen where the next enquiry gets quoted or turned into an order (Setumani can open it but only read it); a stage box to the orders board, filtered, where Santosh, Setumani or Murali move the order along; the lapsing-holds list to whoever can extend or release a hold before the slabs unreserve themselves (Santosh or Setumani — Murali can only look); the dispatch figure to Setumani or Santosh on the Dispatch Check, or to Raghav and Murali on Packing Lists; and the advance figure to whoever can clear it — Setumani, Murali or Santosh typing the receipt onto the order's Receipts card, or Santosh alone waiving it in writing so the load can leave. Raghav's path out of this screen is the orders list and the activity feed, from which he opens the order and works its checklist, invoice and challan.

entry.title: Enquiries — logging what a customer asked for, and turning it into an order
entry.purpose: This is the book of everything customers have asked us for, written down from the mail or call that brought it, before there is any order. Its second job is the hand-off: an enquiry that has a real customer saved against it becomes a draft internal sales order in one click, carrying its lines, the customer's standing terms and a part-answered SOP checklist with it.
entry.whoActs: Santosh and Murali write here — they log a new enquiry, edit it, add and remove lines, move its status, assign it and convert it. Setumani can open the screen and read everything, but every field is greyed and the buttons are gone: no "Save enquiry", no "Undo changes", no "Assign to me" or "Unassign", no per-line Save or remove, no grey Add row at the foot of the lines table, and no status buttons. The "Where it stands" and "Convert to order" boxes both just say "Read only for this login." Raghav does not get this screen at all: there is no Enquiries row in his sidebar, and typing the address gives him the refusal page. The bay 5 dispatch team has one screen only; Enquiries is not in their sidebar and the address is refused before the page opens.
steps: Open Enquiries from the sidebar, or from the "Open enquiries" tile on the Commercial overview. It opens on Open, which is New plus Quoted — the ones nobody has finished answering. The chips across the top (Open, New, Quoted, Ordered, Lost, Closed, All) each carry their own count, and the counts do not change when you click a chip, so you can always see how many are sitting in each state.

Find an existing one with the Search box: it matches the enquiry number, the customer's name, a prospect's name, the subject line, or the contact person's name. Press Search or Enter — typing alone does not filter. A Clear button appears once a search has run and puts the list back. The foot of the list says how many enquiries matched; Previous / Next appear only when there is more than one page of 50.
To log a new one, press "Log an enquiry" (top right). Santosh and Murali get the form; Setumani is turned away at this point even though she can see the button.

On the form, under "Who it is from": search the customer master by name, e-mail or customer code and pick the customer. The picked customer sits in a grey strip showing their code, city and country, with an "open" link to their record and a "change" link to swap them out. If they are not on the master yet — normal for a first enquiry — leave it blank and type the Prospect name instead; the search offers to add the customer first if you would rather. Picking a customer greys the Prospect name box and labels it "(not used — a customer is picked)".

Fill the contact person, their e-mail and phone. These are what the SOP checklist later prints as the customer contact, so they are worth typing even when the customer is on the master. They can all be left empty, but a half-typed e-mail address will be refused.

Under "The enquiry": set Received (defaults to today), How it arrived (EMAIL by default, or PHONE, WHATSAPP, VISIT, WEBSITE, REFERRAL, OTHER), a Subject, and paste the mail — or write down what was said on the phone — into "What they said".

Leave "Assign to me" ticked if you are going to answer it. Leave the Number box blank and the ERP issues the next one for the financial year (ENQ/26-27/N0001 and so on). Only type a number when you are mirroring one that already exists elsewhere.

Under "What they asked for": three blank rows are waiting. Each row takes our Design, the Customer SKU, Thickness (the box suggests 1.2 cm, 2 cm, 3 cm and 7 mm, and anything you type such as "20mm" is stored as "2 cm"), Finish, Slabs, Sq ft and Notes. "Add a line" gives you more rows and each row has its own "remove"; rows left completely blank are thrown away, so you do not have to clear the spares.
Press "Log the enquiry" (Cancel beside it goes back to the list without saving). It saves and opens the enquiry's own page.

On the enquiry page the header carries the number, its status badge, an amber "Prospect" badge if no customer is attached yet, and a line giving who it is from, the date it came in, how it arrived, and whether it is assigned. That last word is only "assigned" or "assigned to you" — the screen never names the other person it is assigned to. "Assign to me" / "Unassign" sit next to "All enquiries".

Correct anything in the left-hand panel and press "Save enquiry"; a green "Saved." strip confirms it. "Undo changes" puts the fields back to the last saved version. This is also where you attach the real customer once they have been added to the master — pick them, then Save.

Work the lines in the table at the bottom, which says how many lines there are. Each existing line has its own Save and remove; the grey row at the end is a new line with an Add button. Removing a line renumbers the rest, so there is never a gap.

Move the enquiry in the "Where it stands" box: "Mark quoted" once a quote has gone out, "Back to new", or "Close" for one that was dropped or duplicated. The button for the status it is already on is not shown at all. To mark it lost, type the reason in the box first — the Mark lost button stays greyed until you do.

When it is a real order, use the "Convert to order" box. Choose the order kind — it pre-picks Domestic (DTA) if the customer's country reads India and Export for everyone else — and press "Create the order". The screen jumps straight to the new draft order.

After conversion the enquiry page shows a green line naming the order it became, with a link to it and its kind and state in brackets — "This enquiry became ORD/26-27/N0007 (export, draft)." The status card is replaced by "The order carries this enquiry now." and the convert box by "Already converted."
refusals: Saving a new enquiry with neither a customer nor a prospect name: the form says "Pick the customer, or give the prospect's name." before it sends anything, and the ERP itself says "Attach a client or give the prospect's name." An enquiry from nobody cannot be followed up — there would be no one to answer.
Clearing the customer on an existing enquiry and leaving the prospect name blank too: "Keep a client or the prospect's name on the enquiry." Same reason, guarding an edit rather than a first save.

Converting a lost or closed enquiry: "This enquiry is lost; set it back to New first." (or "…is closed…"). The Convert box stays on screen with the button live, so this one is easy to walk into — a change of mind has to be put on the record before an order comes out of it, so the count of lost business stays honest.

Marking lost without a reason: the Mark lost button is greyed until something is typed in the box; if it is reached anyway the ERP says "Say why the enquiry was lost." It is the one question that gets asked months later — price, lead time, went to another supplier — and nobody remembers it if it was not typed at the time.

A new line with neither our design nor the customer's SKU: "Name the design or the customer's SKU on each line." On the logging form it numbers the row — "Line 3: Name the design or the customer's SKU on each line." — and nothing is saved until it is fixed, so a half-typed table never half-lands. A line naming neither describes nothing. Note this is only checked when a line is first added: an existing line can be saved with both boxes emptied.
Pressing Add on the grey new-line row with nothing typed in it: "Fill the line first."
A fractional or negative slab count: "Slabs must be a whole number, zero or more." — and text in the box: "Slabs must be a number." Slabs are counted, not measured.
A negative or non-numeric area: "Sq ft cannot be negative." / "Sq ft must be a number." This figure becomes the order's quantity, so it cannot be nonsense.
A contact e-mail that is not an address: "\"ravi.kumar\" is not an e-mail address." That address is what the quote and the documents are sent to. Leaving it blank is fine; half-filling it is not.

Converting an enquiry with no customer saved on it: on screen this shows as the greyed "Create the order" button and the amber warning under the picker, "An order needs a customer here. Pick one (or add it on the customers page) before converting." If it is attempted anyway the ERP spells out the fix: "Attach a client before converting: an order needs a client on the master. Open the enquiry, pick the client (or create one from the prospect's details), save, then convert." An order has to be raised against a real customer — the invoice, the packing list and the challan all take their party details from that record, so there is nowhere for a prospect-only order to get them.

Converting one that has already been converted: "Enquiry ENQ/26-27/N0012 is already order ORD/26-27/N0007." It names the order so you can go to it instead of making a second one for the same request. On screen the convert box has already been replaced by "Already converted."

Changing the customer on an enquiry that has become an order: the picker is greyed and the note under it reads "The order carries the customer now; it cannot be changed here." (the ERP's own words, if it is forced, are "This enquiry has become an order; its client cannot be changed here."). The order is already carrying that customer into the PI and the invoice.

Three rules exist that this screen simply does not give you a button for, so you will not meet their messages in normal work — but they are the reason certain buttons are missing. There is no "Mark ordered": Ordered is only ever written by Convert ("Use Convert to order — it creates the order and marks the enquiry Ordered."), so an enquiry can never claim an order that does not exist. Once converted, no status buttons are shown at all ("This enquiry has become an order; its status follows the order now."), because the order is the live record from there and two statuses drifting apart would mean nobody knows which is true. And the button for the status the enquiry is already on is hidden rather than refused ("Already Quoted.").
Typing a number by hand that already exists: "Enquiry number ENQ/26-27/N0004 already exists". Two enquiries with one number cannot be told apart later.
Picking a customer that has since been removed from the master: "That client is not on the master."

Setumani, or anyone read-only, reaching the logging form: the form will not open — she gets the page that says "Your login is not allowed to open /office/commercial/enquiries/new" with a "Go to my start page" button. On the enquiry itself she sees "Read only for this login." in the status and convert boxes. Raghav gets the same refusal for /office/commercial/enquiries — enquiries are not his desk; he picks the work up at the checklist, the invoice and the challan.
gotchas: Setumani sees a full-colour "Log an enquiry" button on the list, but pressing it bounces her to the refusal page — the button is not hidden for read-only logins. She reads enquiries; Santosh or Murali logs them.

"Create the order" stays greyed until a customer is SAVED onto the enquiry. Picking one in the search box is not enough — press "Save enquiry" first, then the button lights up. The amber line under the picker ("An order needs a customer here…") is the warning that this has not been done.
Pressing Search is required. Typing in the search box on its own changes nothing; the list only re-filters when you press Search or Enter.

The search does not look inside "What they said" or the contact's e-mail address. It matches the number, the customer, the prospect, the subject and the contact person's name only — so put anything you will want to find again into the Subject.
The chip counts ignore which chip you have clicked, but they do follow the search box: run a search and the counts drop to what matched. Clear the search to see the true totals again.
The "Open" chip is New + Quoted together. An enquiry you closed or lost disappears from the default view; use the Closed, Lost or All chips to find it.

If you arrived from a customer's own page the list is filtered to that customer and a "Show every customer" button appears; until you press it you are looking at one customer's enquiries, not the book.

Thickness is silently standardised. Type "20mm" and it is stored as "2 cm"; the PI and the invoice each print it their own way. Do not re-type it to look different — it will change back. Anything that is not close to 7 mm, 1.2 cm, 2 cm or 3 cm is kept exactly as you typed it.

The line number in a refusal counts only the rows that were sent, not the rows on screen. Blank rows are dropped first, so if the first row is empty and the second is wrong, the message says "Line 1". A row is not blank if anything at all is in it — a row with only a note or only a quantity is sent, and is then refused for having no design or SKU.
The enquiry page never names who an enquiry is assigned to. It says "assigned" (or "assigned to you") and nothing more, so if you need to know whose it is, ask.

Editing an enquiry's lines AFTER it has been converted changes nothing on the order. The order took its own copy at the moment of conversion. Corrections after that point belong on the order screen, not here.

Conversion is one-way and there is no confirmation step. Pressing "Create the order" immediately issues an order number, writes the draft order, marks the enquiry Ordered and navigates away. There is no undo button on this screen.

Order kind is decided by the customer's country field, which is free text on the master. Only a country reading "India" pre-picks Domestic; blank, misspelt, abbreviated to "IN", or foreign all pre-pick Export. Check the dropdown before converting — correcting it afterwards on the order is more work than picking it right here.

A number typed by hand does not advance the ERP's counter, by design (a mirrored number must not consume one of ours). Leave the Number box blank unless you are deliberately mirroring — and if you are, copy the number off the paper in front of you rather than the greyed example in the box, which is written without the N our own numbers carry.
Blank line rows on the logging form are thrown away, so the three rows that appear by default cost nothing if you only need one.
An enquiry can be saved with no lines at all. It will convert, but the order it becomes will have no lines either — the screen says so under an empty table.
After conversion you can still correct the contact details, subject, prospect name, date and notes on the enquiry; only the customer and the status are locked.

The lost reason cannot be edited once it is set — the box disappears and the reason shows as a plain line — and it is wiped if you later move the enquiry back to New or Quoted. Closing a lost enquiry keeps it.
entry.handsTo: Converting hands the work to the Orders stage. A draft internal sales order is created and opened on screen, numbered in its own series (ORD/26-27/N0007 and so on): it carries the enquiry's lines renumbered from one, with the sq ft as the quantity and a description built from design-finish-thickness; the customer's currency, incoterm, payment and delivery terms, port of discharge, bill-to, consignee and notify party copied from their record — and where the customer names no currency, rupees for a domestic order and dollars for an export; and the SOP checklist already filled in for every point an enquiry can answer. What is deliberately left blank for the order desk is the customer's PO number and its evidence, the rates and order value, samples, the delivery schedule, special packing, the forwarder and the receiver. The order is stamped with who created it, carries a note saying which enquiry it came from, and opens its history with a line recording the same. Setumani picks it up from there — pricing the lines, checking stock and raising the PI — while the enquiry itself goes quiet, showing only a green link to the order it became.

entry.title: Customers — the customer master
entry.purpose: This is the one place Pacific keeps a customer: who they are, how to reach them, their GSTIN, PAN and state code, their customer code, and the exact address blocks that print on the proforma, the invoice and the packing list. Everything downstream — a new order's terms, the bill-to and consignee on the documents, the tax the invoice charges — is copied from here at the moment the customer is picked, so what is typed on this screen is what the customer eventually reads on paper.
entry.whoActs: Santosh (manager) and Murali (logistics) can add customers and change them. Setumani (executive) and Raghav (documents) can open the screen and read every field, but for them the "New customer", "Save customer", "Undo changes" and "Mark inactive" buttons are not shown at all and every box is greyed out — they look, they do not type. The bay 5 dispatch team never reaches this screen; if they somehow open it they are sent straight back to their Dispatch Check screen. Note the screen is headed "Customers" but the sidebar row says "Clients" — same thing. The master is shared with International Sales, so a customer you are about to add may already be on it from their side.
steps: Open the screen from the sidebar row "Clients". The list is in name order, A to Z, one row per customer: name (with the e-mail underneath), customer code, place (city and country), GSTIN, contact person and phone, and a count of how many enquiries and how many orders that customer already has. 50 rows at a time, with a running total at the bottom; Previous / Next appear there only when there is more than one page.

To find somebody, type into the Search box and press the Search button (or Enter). It matches the name, the e-mail address and the customer code — nothing else — and part of a word is enough. A "Clear" button appears next to it once a search is running.
Inactive customers are hidden. Tick "Show inactive" to see them; they appear with an amber "Inactive" tag.

To add one, press "New customer" (Santosh and Murali only). A panel opens above the list with the full form, and the button itself turns into "Cancel" while the panel is open. Only the name is compulsory — everything else can be filled in later. Press "Add customer" to save, or "Cancel" to drop it. The new customer appears in the list straight away with a green line, "Barlow Stone Ltd was added."

To open a customer, click their name. The top of their page shows the name, an Active or Inactive tag, then the code, city, country and the date they were added (or "No code or place on file" when none of those are filled), an "All customers" button back to the list, and — for Santosh and Murali — a "Mark inactive" button.

Fill the first block, Customer: Name (compulsory), Customer code (prints on the customer's copies of the export paperwork, e.g. USA-041), Contact person, E-mail, Phone, CC e-mails (separate with commas, semicolons or new lines), City, Country, State code, and a free-text Address box, one line per line.

Fill the second block, Tax and defaults: GSTIN, PAN, Default currency, Default incoterm, Default delivery terms, Default payment terms, Default port of discharge, and a Notes box for anything the next person should know. These defaults are what a new order for this customer opens with.

Fill the third block, Printed address blocks: Bill to, Ship to / consignee, and Notify party. Each is a plain typing box — the FIRST line is the party's name as it should print, every line after it is an address line. They are designed to be pasted straight out of the customer's e-mail and then tidied. Leave Ship to blank and the Bill to block is used as the consignee; leave Notify party blank and none prints; leave a block empty altogether and the module prints the plain Address from the first block instead.
Press "Save customer". A green "Saved." line confirms it. "Undo changes" puts the boxes back to the last saved version — it does not undo a save that has already happened.

At the bottom of a customer's page are two panels, Enquiries and Orders. The heading shows the true total; the list underneath shows the newest 20 of each — enquiry number with its subject, status and date; order number with its type and currency, status and date — and a "See all" link to that customer's filtered list.
refusals: Saving with the name box empty. On the new-customer panel: "Give the customer a name." On an existing customer: "The customer needs a name." (the same refusal can also come back worded "Name is required." or "Name cannot be blank."). A customer with no name would print a blank party block on an invoice, so the name is the one thing that can never be missing.

A GSTIN that is not shaped like a GSTIN. The message quotes back what was typed, in capitals: "33AALCP2750N1Z" does not look like a GSTIN (15 characters: 2-digit state code, the 10-character PAN, an entity digit, Z, a check character). This catches a PAN, a phone number or a half-pasted string dropped into the GSTIN box. It checks the SHAPE only — a typo in the last character will still pass, so read it back against the customer's paperwork.

A PAN that is not shaped like a PAN: "AALCP275ON" does not look like a PAN (5 letters, 4 digits, 1 letter). Same reason — it stops the wrong number being filed under PAN, it does not verify the number is real.

A state code that is not exactly two digits: State code "3" must be the two-digit GST state code (Tamil Nadu is 33). Two digits is the shape the GST state code has, it prints on the invoice, and it is the field the tax rule reads to say which state the buyer is in — so a one-digit or three-digit entry is meaningless there.

A desk that only reads trying to save anyway — for instance a page left open when a login is changed: "Not available for this login." If the login has been signed out or switched off in the background: "Please sign in." If the customer has been removed or the link is stale: "Client not found." Other save or load failures come back as "Could not save the customer", "Could not save", "Could not change this", "Could not load the customer master" or "Could not load the customer".

NOT a refusal, and this surprises people: a name that already exists is allowed through. The screen says so in grey next to the Add button — "A name that already exists is allowed — you will be told, not stopped" — and after saving it shows an amber line. Adding from the list: "A client named JB Homes Pvt Ltd already exists — check it is not the same customer before you raise an order." Renaming an existing customer into a name already on the master warns too, on their own page, worded "...already exists — check it is not the same customer twice." Two legal entities can trade under one name, and the person typing is the one who knows which is which.

Also NOT available: there is no Delete anywhere on this screen. A customer who has stopped buying is marked inactive instead. The master is shared with International Sales and every past invoice, proforma and packing list points back at these rows, so nothing is ever removed.
gotchas: Fill in the tax details and address blocks BEFORE raising an order. An order takes its copy of the bill-to, consignee, notify party, currency, incoterm, delivery terms, payment terms and port of discharge at the moment the customer is picked, and from then on the order keeps its own copy. Correcting a GSTIN here later does NOT correct an order, proforma, invoice or packing list already raised — those have to be fixed on the document itself.

One exception worth knowing: a GSTIN or state code added here after the order but before the invoice is raised still reaches that invoice, because the invoice reads the master as it is on the day it is first raised. Once the invoice exists, it is frozen like everything else.

"Save customer" writes every box on the form, including the empty ones. Emptying a box on screen empties it in the record. There is no partial save, so do not clear a field you are unsure about just to tidy the screen.

"Mark inactive" is a button of its own and saves the moment it is clicked, with no confirmation. It cannot happen by accident from a normal save. It is reversible — the button becomes "Make active". The confirmation spells out what it does not do: "Customer marked inactive — it stays on every document already raised."

Marking a customer inactive also takes them out of every box that picks a customer — the enquiry, the new order, the challan consignee search and the customer list on the design codes screen all show active customers only. If a colleague says a customer has vanished from their search box, look here with "Show inactive" ticked and make them active again.

Search only looks at name, e-mail and customer code. Typing a GSTIN, a phone number, a city or a contact person's name returns "No customer matches …" even though the customer is sitting there. Search on the name or the code.
The list hides inactive customers unless "Show inactive" is ticked, and the count at the bottom says "(active)" when it is filtering. A customer you cannot find may simply be inactive.
The state code fills itself in from the GSTIN only when the State code box is left empty. If a wrong code is already typed, it stays and the GSTIN does not override it.

As Pacific is set up today, every domestic invoice charges IGST at 18% whatever the buyer's state code says, and no "state code missing" warning is raised — that is an admin setting in Settings, which nobody on this desk can change. The state code still prints on the invoice and is the field the tax rule would read if that setting were ever turned off, so keep it right; just do not expect a wrong or missing one to show up as a warning on Raghav's invoices.

The customer code is forced into capitals when saved, whatever case it was typed in. Nothing checks it for duplicates either — only the NAME is compared against the master — so two customers can end up sharing a code without anyone being told.

A customer added with nothing but a name has no GSTIN, no PAN and no printed address blocks. Their documents print the plain Address lines instead of a proper Bill to block, and the GSTIN cell on the invoice is empty. The same is true of customers that came across from International Sales — none of the tax fields or address blocks exist for them until somebody fills them in here.

Country matters more than it looks: "India" (in any spelling of case, and "IN" or "Bharat" too) is what makes the enquiry's Convert button offer a domestic order rather than an export one, and a domestic order is the one that carries GST. A blank Country counts as export.
Raghav can see a customer's enquiry numbers listed at the bottom of their page, but clicking one takes him to a "no access" page — enquiries are not his desk. He should use the order links instead.
"Undo changes" reverts the boxes to the last loaded or saved version only. Once "Save customer" has gone through there is no undo — retype the old value.
entry.handsTo: The customer record feeds the rest of the line. Murali or Santosh log an enquiry and pick the customer off this master; an enquiry with nobody on it cannot be converted, and the enquiry screen says so — "An order needs a customer here. Pick one (or add it on the customers page) before converting." If the search box there finds nothing it offers the same way out: "No customer matches. Leave this blank and fill the prospect's details below, or add the customer first." Converting that enquiry, or raising a new order, copies the bill-to, consignee, notify party, currency, incoterm, delivery and payment terms and port of discharge straight onto the order's Parties panel, where Setumani can still edit them before anything prints — the panel itself says "Prefilled from the client master … edit it now rather than on the document." From there the same blocks print on the proforma, on Raghav's tax invoice (which also takes the GSTIN, state code and customer code from here) and on the packing list. Murali's delivery challans can pull a consignee name, address and GSTIN off this master rather than being typed by hand, and a customer's own item codes and barcodes on the design codes screen hang off these same rows. So the practical rule is: get the customer right here first, then start the order.

entry.title: Orders — the order book and the order page
entry.purpose: This is where a customer's purchase order becomes Pacific's own internal sales order: one numbered record per deal, carrying the client, the agreed terms, the party addresses that will print on the proforma and the invoice, the lines being sold, the money received, and the 22-point internal sales order checklist. Everything later in the module — the stock hold, the proforma, the packing list, the dispatch check, the invoice and the challan — hangs off the order created here, and the order page is the one screen that shows the whole deal in one place.
entry.whoActs: Santosh (manager) writes everything here, and he alone may cancel an order, waive the advance, or lower the advance percentage. Setumani (executive) creates and edits orders, lines, terms, receipts and the checklist freely — everything except cancelling, approving and waiving. Murali (logistics) also creates and edits orders in full, and he may delete a receipt; he may NOT stamp the checklist "Approved" — his Approve button looks live but the order refuses it (see the refusals). Raghav (documents) may OPEN any order and read the whole of it; the order itself is not his to edit. His writable parts of this screen are the checklist points and the order-tasks list, plus the Invoice tab. Bay 5 never reaches this screen at all: a dispatch-team login that types the address is sent straight back to the Dispatch Check. A read-only desk sees the same screen with the same layout, not a reduced one — and on this screen several of Raghav's buttons look enabled and are refused when pressed, because the screen reads his general permission rather than his permission on orders.
steps: Open Orders. The top card is the stage board: one tile per stage — Draft, Confirmed, Stock checked, PI issued, Packing, Dispatch check, Ready, Invoiced, Dispatched, Closed, Cancelled — each with a count. Click a tile to show only those orders; click it again, or the 'Showing … · clear' link, to go back. Under the tiles a line says how many orders are short of Closed and reminds you that only three moves are gated: the PI waits for the stock check, the invoice for the approval, dispatch for the advance.

Find an order with the search box (order number, customer PO number or client name — it waits until you stop typing), and narrow by Export / Domestic / Both. There is a Refresh button beside them. The table shows the order number with its date and who raised it, the client and country, kind, stage, customer PO and its date, currency and incoterm, the number of lines with a shorthand of what hangs off it (H = holds, PI = proformas, PL = packing lists, INV = invoices), and when it last changed. 50 orders to a page; a running count and Previous / Next appear underneath once there are more than 50. Whatever you filtered to stays in the address bar, so a filtered list can be sent to somebody.

Start a new order with the 'New order' button (top right of the list). It only appears for a desk that may write; Raghav's login shows the button but is quietly returned to the order book if he uses it.

On the New order form, pick the kind first: Export (priced in USD, shipping from the standard port of loading) or Domestic (priced in rupees, DTA invoice, GST by the buyer's state). Leave 'Order number override' blank and the order takes the next number from the counter; type one only when you are matching a number raised elsewhere.

Pick the client by typing a few letters and choosing from the list. Choosing the client fills in, but never overwrites, what the client master already knows: currency, incoterm, payment and delivery terms, port of discharge, customer contact, destination country, and the Bill to / Consignee / Notify blocks. 'Buyer, if not the consignee' is never prefilled. 'Change' puts you back to the search box. If no client matches there is a link to go and add one.

Fill what you have: the salesperson the proforma is being raised for; the customer's PO number and date and what evidence is held for the order (their purchase order, our proforma acknowledged, or an email naming items, quantity, rate and terms); the commercial terms (currency, incoterm, payment mode, delivery terms, payment terms, and the advance percentage that must be in before the truck leaves); the four party blocks; the routing (pre-carriage, place of receipt, port of loading and discharge, final destination, countries); the delivery schedule, special packing or markings, forwarder, nominated receiver, customer contact, and internal notes that print on nothing. On this form, anything left blank takes the standard default for the kind of order or the client's own answer — blank is not an instruction to clear.

Press 'Create order'. The button stays grey until a client is picked, and a line under the form says 'Pick a client to create the order.' until you do. The order is numbered, the checklist is filled in from your answers, and you land on the order page itself. The lines are NOT on this form — they are added on the order.

On the order page, read the top block: order number, Export/Domestic badge, current stage badge, order date, client and country, customer PO and date, the enquiry it came from if any, currency, and who raised it. A cancelled order also shows its reason in red.

Under that is the Pipeline card. Three badges say what the gates can see: whether stock is held right now, whether the checklist is approved and by whom, and the advance as a figure ('Advance short USD 3,000.00 — USD 0.00 of USD 3,000.00', 'Advance in: …', 'No advance asked', or 'Advance waived'). Then the stage tiles, each showing the date it was reached, or a dash. At the foot of the card: when the order was created, when it last changed, and who checked and approved the checklist.

Move the order by clicking the stage you have reached, after optionally typing a note in 'Note for the next move'. The stages are not a queue — any stage may be entered whenever the work is actually done, and three of them are gated (see the refusals). The tile for the stage the order is already on is not clickable, and on a finished order every tile is dead and the note box and the Cancel button are gone, replaced by 'This order has finished its pipeline.' Entering a stage stamps today's date against it; earlier stamps are never wiped, so an order sent back to Packing after a failed dispatch check keeps the date it was first checked.

Understand the stage names: Draft is a new order still being typed; Confirmed means the customer's order is accepted; Stock checked means slabs are held against it; PI issued means the proforma has gone out; Packing means the packing list is being built; Dispatch check means bay 5 is looking at the packed slabs; Ready means they passed; Invoiced means the final invoice is raised; Dispatched means the goods have left; Closed is finished — and closing also marks every slab still reserved against the order as dispatched; Cancelled is a side exit, not a step on the strip, and needs a written reason.

Open the Items tab and build the lines. Each row takes design, customer SKU, description, thickness (type it, or pick from the suggestions that drop down), finish, size, grade, number of slabs, quantity, unit, rate, amount, HSN, a 'sample' tick, and a note. The bottom row of the table is the new line — fill it and press 'Add line'; that button stays grey until the row has a design, a description or a customer SKU. An existing row's Save button lights up only once you have changed something. Delete removes the line at once, with no confirmation, and renumbers the rest. Leave Amount empty and it is worked out as quantity × rate (the figure is previewed under the box); type an amount and exactly that figure stands, for orders whose agreed total is not the multiplication.

Read the Totals card under the lines: number of lines split into goods and samples, total slabs ('what the stock check has to find'), quantity per unit, and the order value, which is the figure the advance percentage is taken from. Sample lines are shaded in the table and counted again in a line of their own.

Back on Overview, correct the header in place — including the client (which re-fills the party blocks and terms from the new client and shows 'unsaved' until you save), the kind, the selling company whose proforma this order will raise, and an exchange rate box used for an export invoice priced in rupee terms. The order number itself is shown but locked. 'Save header' sits at the top of the card and only wakes up once something has changed; 'Discard changes' appears beside it while there is something to discard. Here, unlike the new-order form, clearing a box clears the field — except currency and country of origin, which keep their current value.

Record money on the Receipts card: kind (Advance, CAD, Balance, Other), amount, currency, the date it arrived, mode, reference and notes. 'Record receipt' stays grey until there is an amount and a date, and the date box will not offer a day in the future. Three boxes above show the advance asked, the advance received and what is still short, and each receipt row says whether it counted toward the advance and, if not, why. The same card carries the waiver: 'Waive the advance…' with a reason, and 'Lift the waiver' to put the gate back — both the manager's.

Work the checklist at the bottom of Overview: 22 SOP rows, numbered 1 to 19 (point 1 has three sub-lines), each with the answer recorded and a 'settled' tick. Points the order can answer are filled in automatically and refilled after every edit, and an answer typed by hand is never overwritten (blank a point and the order's own answer comes back). Open points are shaded amber and counted — 'go back to the sender for these before the PI'. 'Save answers' appears once you have changed something, 'Mark checked' stamps prepared-and-checked in your name (it reads 'Check again' afterwards), and 'Approve' stamps the approval the final invoice waits for.

Below the checklist, tick off the order tasks — container booking, CHA, BL draft, COO, CEFA, fumigation, the portal uploads, transport and e-way bill on a domestic order — each with a date and a note, or marked 'Not required' (which then reads 'Needed after all'). The date box only opens once the task is ticked. There is also a box at the foot to add a task this order needs that is not on the standard list. Ticked and not-required lines drop into a second group underneath.

Use the other tabs across the top for the rest of the deal: Stock, Proforma, Packing, Invoice, Documents and Log, each showing a count of what it holds. Documents is the export workbook and only fills up on an export order with an export invoice; the order-tasks list appears there too, because most of it is Raghav's work. The Log lists every stage move, edit, hold, proforma, packing list, receipt and invoice with who did it and when, can be narrowed with the 'Show' dropdown, and opens the fine detail of any line on request; the first hundred entries are already loaded and the pager reaches the rest.
refusals: Creating an order without a client — the Create button stays grey and the form says 'Pick a client to create the order.' (the order itself answers 'Pick a client' if the request ever reaches it). The order's terms, addresses and documents are all read off the client; there is nothing to raise an order against without one.

Typing an order number that has already been used — 'Order number ORD/26-27/N0001 already exists'. Hand-typed numbers do not advance the counter, so two people typing the same one is entirely possible, and two orders with one number would break every document that quotes it.

Adding a line with nothing to identify it — the Add line button stays grey with 'A new line needs at least a design, a description or a customer SKU' under the table, and the order answers 'A line needs a design, a description or a customer SKU' if it is sent anyway. A nameless line cannot be picked from stock, packed, or printed on a proforma.

Typing letters into quantity or rate — 'Quantity must be a number' / 'Rate must be a number'. A quantity that will not parse silently becomes nothing, and the order value, the advance and the checklist all come off those figures.
Typing letters into the exchange rate on the header — 'Exchange rate must be a number'; and an advance percentage outside 0 to 100 — 'Advance required must be a percentage between 0 and 100'.

Moving to PI issued with no live stock hold — 'Stock check first: place a hold before issuing the PI'. The owner's rule is stock check before PI: a proforma promises specific slabs, so they must be held first. Note the hold must still be live — an expired hold reads as no hold at all.

Moving to Invoiced before the checklist is approved — 'The checklist must be approved before the final invoice'. Two signatures, two people: Commercial prepares and checks the sheet, the manager approves it, and the final invoice waits for that approval.

Moving to Dispatched before the advance is in — 'The advance has not been received: the truck does not leave before it', followed by the figures, e.g. 'Advance short USD 3,000.00 — USD 0.00 of USD 3,000.00'. Packing and loading may happen before the money; the truck leaving may not. The greyed Dispatched tile carries the same sentence on the screen, before you click.

Moving to Dispatched on an order whose lines are not priced — 'The order has no total yet, so the 30% advance cannot be worked out: price the line items, or waive the advance.' A percentage of nothing is not an amount, so the gate cannot tell whether the money is in.

Moving a finished order — 'A closed order cannot move' / 'A cancelled order cannot move'. On screen you do not get that far: every tile is dead and the card says 'This order has finished its pipeline.' Closed and Cancelled are the end; reopening by moving would leave the automatic dispatch of the closed order's slabs unexplained.
Two people moving the same order at once — 'The order moved meanwhile — reload and try again'. Only one move lands, so the log never records a move from a stage the order had already left.

Cancelling as anyone but the manager — 'Only the Commercial Manager or an admin cancels an order' (the red 'Cancel order…' button is visible but disabled, with that line under it). Cancelling kills a numbered document the customer has seen.

Cancelling without saying why — 'Give a reason for cancelling'; the confirm button stays grey until the reason box has something in it. Three months later somebody will ask why this order died, and the reason is stored with the cancellation in one write so it can never go missing.

Approving the checklist without the right login — 'Only the Commercial Manager or an admin approves'. Setumani and Raghav see the Approve button disabled with that line beside it. MURALI IS THE TRAP: his login holds the approving permission generally, so his button looks live, but the order refuses him with the same sentence. Approval is the second signature the final invoice depends on; on this screen it is the manager's or an admin's only.

Setting the advance percentage to 0 — 'Setting the advance to 0% asks for no money before dispatch at all — that is a waiver of the 30% this order asks for, without the reason a waiver carries. Only the Commercial Manager or an admin may do that — or waive the advance on the receipts card, which asks for a reason in writing and is logged.' Typing 0 in a header box would open the truck with no reason, no name and nothing in the log.

Lowering the advance percentage at all — including clearing the box so it falls back to a lower standard figure, or changing the kind so the standard figure drops (Domestic asks 100%, Export 30%, so Domestic → Export is a lowering) — 'Lowering the advance from 100% to 30% opens dispatch on money that has not arrived, the way a waiver does. Only the Commercial Manager or an admin may do that…'. Raising it, or leaving it alone, is an ordinary edit.

Waiving the advance from the wrong desk — 'Only the Commercial Manager or an admin waives the advance' (button visible, disabled, reason beside it) — and waiving with no reason — 'Give a reason for waiving the advance'. The waiver is the one way past the module's only payment gate, so it costs a name, a reason and a log line. Lifting a waiver that is not there answers 'The advance is not waived on this order'.

Recording money or waiving on a finished order — 'This order is closed or cancelled; receipts cannot be recorded on it' / '…the advance cannot be waived on it'. The entry form is replaced by that sentence rather than failing after you type. There is no truck left to release, and the month's reconciliation would have to explain the figure. Lifting a waiver is still allowed after closing, so a waiver stamped on the wrong order can be taken off.

Back-to-front receipt details — 'Amount must be more than zero, with at most 2 decimals' and 'Received on cannot be in the future'. Money is recorded once it has arrived, and a third decimal on a receipt is almost always a slipped key that the bank statement will not match.

Deleting a receipt from the wrong desk — Setumani and Raghav see no Delete buttons at all, with the line 'Only the Commercial Manager or an admin deletes a receipt.' under the table. Removing the only advance closes dispatch again, so it is not a clerk's click.

Putting a date on a task that is not ticked — the date box stays shut and says 'The date is the day the task was done — tick it first'; sent anyway, the order answers 'Only a task marked done carries a date'. Adding a task the order already has — '"Container booking" is already on this order's task list'; adding one with no name — 'Give the task a name'.

Raghav saving anything on the order itself (the header, a line, a stage move, a receipt) — 'Not available for this login.' His Save, Add line and Record receipt buttons look live because the screen reads his general permission rather than his permission on orders, but the order is refused when it is sent. His writable parts of this screen are the checklist points and the order tasks.
Opening an order that has been removed, or a mistyped link — 'Order not found'. Likewise 'Line not found on this order' and 'Receipt not found on this order' when two people delete the same row.

Clearing the currency or country of origin on the order page — nothing happens; the hint on the currency box says 'Cannot be blank — a blank box keeps the current currency' and the country of origin box says 'Cannot be blank — a blank box keeps the current value.' Every document prices in the order's currency, so it can be changed but never emptied.

A client list that will not load — 'Could not read the client list.' shown under the search box, deliberately different from 'No client matches', so nobody raises an order believing a client does not exist when the list simply failed.
entry.handsTo: The order goes next to the Stock tab, where Setumani or Santosh place a hold on the slabs — that is what unlocks the proforma. From there: the Proforma tab (Setumani or Santosh issue the PI), the Packing tab (Setumani or Santosh build the packing list), bay 5's Dispatch Check screen (pass or fail the packed slabs), and then the invoice and the challan — Raghav's usual work, though Setumani and Santosh may raise them too, and Murali may raise a challan — with the final invoice waiting for the approved checklist. Money recorded on the Receipts card is what eventually releases the truck. Every one of those steps also drags the order's own stage forward by itself — a hold placed marks it Stock checked, a proforma issued marks it PI issued, a packing list submitted marks it Packing, a verified list marks it Dispatch check and then Ready, an invoice issued marks it Invoiced, slabs dispatched mark it Dispatched — so the board usually keeps itself up to date without anyone clicking a stage. A rejected dispatch check is the one automatic move backwards: it returns the order to Packing. Closing the order at the end also sweeps every slab still reserved against it into dispatched, and after that the order is read-only forever.
gotchas: A greyed stage tile is never a mystery: the reason is printed in amber under the tile's name and repeated if you hover it, and the three badges above the strip (stock held / approved / advance) say which gate is shut before you click anything.
The stages are a record, not a route. Nothing forces Confirmed before Packing, and you may enter a stage the moment the work is done. Only three moves are gated — PI issued, Invoiced, Dispatched.
Dates on the stage tiles are never erased. An order that goes back to Packing after a rejected dispatch check still shows the day it was first checked; the strip is history, not a current position.

Murali's Approve button on the checklist is the one control on this screen that looks live and is not. It is enabled for him but refused when pressed — approval is the manager's or an admin's. Do not plan a month's paperwork around Murali approving.

Blank means two different things in two places. On the New order form a blank box takes the standard default for the kind of order, or the client's own answer. On the order page, clearing a box clears the field — except currency and country of origin, which keep what they had.

'Advance required' blank does not mean no advance. Blank falls back to the standard figure for the kind — 100% domestic, 30% export as it stands — and the box's hint names today's figure and warns that lowering it is the manager's. Zero is the only way to say 'none', and zero is the manager's.
The Amount column is the one to watch. Left empty it is quantity × rate; type a figure and that exact figure is kept, which is how a proforma total the customer agreed to survives untouched.

Delete on a line is immediate — no 'are you sure' — and renumbers everything below it, so line 4 becomes line 3 on every document raised afterwards. Delete on a receipt does ask first, naming the kind and the amount.

A hand-typed order number does not move the counter — the next automatic order still takes the number it was going to take. The order number itself cannot be changed afterwards; the box on the header is locked.

Changing the client on an existing order overwrites the party blocks and the terms with the new client's, and shows 'unsaved' until you save the header. If you have hand-edited an address, re-check it after a client change. 'Buyer, if not the consignee' is the one block a client change leaves alone.

The party blocks print exactly as typed. An empty Notify block prints no notify party, which is why there is a 'Clear' link on each block — a block with only a stray space in it would print as a party.
The row Save buttons on the lines, and 'Save header', only light up when something actually differs from what is stored; a grey Save means nothing has changed, not that you lack permission.

There are two exchange-rate boxes on a deal and they do different jobs. The one on the order header is for an export invoice priced in rupee terms. The one that makes a receipt in another currency count toward the advance is the rate on the order's live INVOICE — until that is typed, the foreign money sits on the card, the row says so in its own words, and the truck stays put.
Deleting a receipt takes Santosh's or Murali's login; Setumani and Raghav see the list without Delete buttons and the line 'Only the Commercial Manager or an admin deletes a receipt.'

Raghav's order screen shows enabled Save, Add line and Record receipt buttons that the system then refuses. Treat the order header, the lines and the receipts as not his; the checklist and the tasks below are, and so is the Invoice tab.

A waiver can be taken back. 'Lift the waiver' puts the payment gate back on, and both the waiver and the lifting are logged with the reason, so nobody has to guess later why one container left unpaid.
Closing the order is the heavy click: it marks every slab still reserved against the order as dispatched, and a closed order can never move again, take a receipt, or be waived.

If a refresh fails while you are working, the screen does not disappear — the last copy stays with a red banner and a 'Try again' button, and anything you have typed is still there. The order may have moved on in the meantime.

The stage counts on the board DO follow your search box and the Export/Domestic filter; they ignore only the stage filter, which is why clicking 'Packing' narrows the table without emptying the board you clicked from.
The order's own number (ORD/…) is not the proforma's number (SAL-ORD/…); the two are different documents and quoting one for the other confuses the customer.

entry.title: Stock check and holds — the Stock tab on an order
entry.purpose: This is where you find out whether the slabs an order asks for are actually standing in finished goods, and then put the order's name on the ones you want so nobody else can pack or sell them. The reservation is temporary — five days unless the owner has changed the standard length — and whatever the yard cannot supply is passed to the plant as a production request. Until stock is held against the order, the proforma invoice cannot be issued, so in practice this is the gate between "the customer has confirmed" and "we can send them a PI".
entry.whoActs: Santosh (manager) and Setumani (executive) are the two people this screen is built for: they can search stock, tick slabs, place holds and release them, and everything works. Murali (logistics) may search stock and read everything — the results, the holds, how many days are left — but may not place or release a hold. Raghav (documents) can open the tab and read the holds and production requests already on the order, but the stock search itself refuses him, so he never gets a list of slabs to tick. THE IMPORTANT PART: the screen does not grey anything out for Murali or Raghav. Both of them see a full, live-looking Hold reference / Days / Note row with a Place hold button, and live Release buttons on an active hold. The controls only refuse when pressed — Murali is told "Not available for this login.", Raghav "You do not have permission to do that." Nobody on the commercial desk can raise a production request or open the planning queue: both are the admin login's, and the buttons and the link are shown to all four of them anyway. Bay 5 never reaches an order screen, so they never see this at all.
steps: Open the order and click the Stock tab. The number beside the tab name is how many holds the order already has; there is no number when it has none.

Look at "Lines to check". Every ordered line is listed with its design, the customer's own code for it, thickness, finish, how many slabs are needed, and how many are already held. Any line ticked "Sample" on the Items tab is left out on purpose — a free trade sample or a display stand is typed in by hand with no design behind it in finished goods, so a stock check on it would always come back empty.

Press "Check stock" on the line you want. The search runs itself using that line's design and thickness, so one click shows stock. (If the line has no design name the button is greyed — go to the Items tab and give it one first.) There is a "Close" button at the top right of the panel that comes up, for when you want the list back.

Read the result. The top right says how many slabs are available, the total square footage and how many batches they sit in. Below, the slabs are grouped by batch, because one batch was cut from one lot and a customer ordering forty slabs wants them to look alike. Each batch shows its count, its square footage and its grade breakdown. The first batch opens itself; the rest stay closed, because a popular design can return twenty.

Narrow the search if you need to: change the design, pick a different thickness (or "Any"), or type a grade, and press "Check stock" again. The grade box is an exact match — type A, not A+ or a range.
Open any other batch with "Show slabs" — or by clicking the batch name — to see each slab's number, grade, bay and frame (so the yard can find it), size in inches and square footage.

Tick the slabs you want. The checkbox on the batch header ticks or clears the whole batch in one click, and shows half-ticked when only some of that batch is picked. The counter along the bottom keeps a running "Picked X of Y needed", the square footage picked, and an amber "N more to pick" or a green "Quantity covered", so you never have to hold the arithmetic in your head. "Clear picks" starts over. If stock is short of the line, a red "Stock is N short of the line" also sits in that bar — it is there for everybody, including the people who cannot do anything about it.

Set the hold up. "Hold reference" is fixed to this order's number and cannot be typed over; the only time it becomes a dropdown is when the order was converted from an enquiry, where you may also choose the enquiry's number. "Days" is blank and shows the standard length as a faint grey number — normally 5 — so leave it alone unless you have a reason. "Note" is free text for the desk, e.g. "Customer to confirm by Friday".

Press "Place hold on N slab(s)". The button stays greyed until you have ticked at least one slab, so you cannot fire it empty. A green line then confirms how many were held and under which reference, and names anything that was skipped or not found. The order moves itself to "Stock checked" and the move is logged with your name.

If stock is short, an amber panel appears: "Stock has 12 slab(s); this line needs 40. 28 short." Press "Raise production request for the shortfall", check the slabs-needed figure (it is filled in from the line), read the in-stock figure beside it, add a note for the planner ("Ship by 20 Sep; same batch preferred"), and press "Raise request" — or "Cancel" to back out. Be warned: today only an admin login is allowed to raise it, so for all four of you this ends in a refusal. Ask an admin to raise it.

Scroll to "Holds on this order" to see every hold: its reference, whether it is active, how many of its slabs are still held, the square footage, how long is left ("36h left", "4 day(s) left", or "lapsed"), the expiry date spelled out, who placed it and when, the note that was typed, and — on a hold that was given back — the reason it was given back.

To give slabs back, open "Slabs" on an active hold, tick the ones to hand back, type a reason (optional) and press "Release N picked" — or press "Release all N" to hand back everything still held. Each slab shows its own state: held, packed or released.

Finally, "Production requests" lists what has been asked of the plant for this order: design, thickness, how many were needed, how many were in stock, how many are short, how many are planned and in what shade, the position in the queue, the status (Queued, Scheduled, In production, Produced, Cancelled), who raised it and when, and the batch the planner has assigned. The list is read-only here — it is a window on the plant's queue, not a way into it.
refusals: "No slab could be held — 4412: marked CTS — not a full slab; not in finished goods: 4501, 4502" — nothing you ticked could actually be reserved, and the message names every reason slab by slab. A slab cut to size will be refused at dispatch, so counting it here would only promise the customer something the lorry cannot carry.

"slab mark could not be read — refused rather than assumed whole" — the system could not confirm whether that slab is whole or cut, so it refuses rather than guessing. Guessing "whole" is the guess that puts already-cut stone on a customer's truck.

"4412: RESERVED → RESERVED not allowed" (shown among the skipped ones) — plain English: somebody got there first and that slab is already on someone else's hold. "PACKED → RESERVED not allowed" means it is already in a crate. Only a genuinely free slab can be held, so two orders can never both be promised the same stone.

"A hold placed here can only be referenced as ORD/26-27/0164 or ENQ/26-27/0088 — \"PSPL/PI/25-26/0042\" belongs to something else." — the reference is not a label, it is ownership. It decides whose slabs may later be released and packed, so a reference borrowed from another team's paperwork would hand this order their reserved stock. That is exactly why the box is fixed rather than typed, and why you will not normally meet this message from this screen.

"This hold has lapsed." / "This hold has been packed." / "This hold has already been released." — you tried to release a hold that is no longer live, almost always because the five days ran out while the page sat open. The hold's chip can still read "active" when this happens (see the gotchas), which is precisely how you end up pressing Release on a dead hold. A spent hold is history; refresh and place a new one.
"Nothing left to release on this hold." — every slab on it has already gone back or been packed. Hard to reach from this screen, because "Release all" greys itself out when there is nothing left.

"Not on this hold: 4412, 4413" — you named slabs that belong to a different hold. The screen will never touch a slab reserved under somebody else's reference, whatever is asked of it. If only some of what you named is off the hold, the release goes through for the rest and the green line says how many were skipped.

"Nothing is short — stock covers the quantity required." — a production request was raised when the yard already has enough. A queue full of requests the plant does not need is a queue the plant stops reading.

"Which design is short?" / "Give the thickness" / "How many slabs are needed?" / "That line is not on this order" — the plant cannot make a slab from a half-filled request, and a request pointed at another order's line would have the shortfall landing on the wrong customer.

"Not available for this login." — what Murali gets when he presses Place hold or Release. Holding stock commits real inventory and re-stages the order, which the owner kept with the two people who answer for it. Murali may look at stock all day; he may not spend it.

"You do not have permission to do that." — what Raghav gets on Place hold or Release, and what ALL FOUR of you get on "Raise request". Raghav has no business on the stock screen at all, and the production queue was kept with the admin login, so the shortfall has to be raised by an admin today.

"The server's answer could not be read (HTTP 403). You may have been signed out." — what Raghav gets when he presses "Check stock". Ignore the words about being signed out: it is a permission refusal wearing the wrong message. The stock screen is simply not his.
"Pick a design to check" — you cleared the design box before searching.

"No available slab of Carrara Royale 2 cm in finished goods." — the search worked; there is genuinely nothing free of that design and thickness. Only whole, sale-approved, uncut slabs count towards that answer.

"Stock check matched more than 50000 slabs — narrow the design before reading further." — a search too broad to answer honestly. It stops and says so rather than quietly showing you the first few thousand and letting you conclude stock is short.

"This order has no stock line yet — add items on the Items tab." / "No stock has been held for this order yet." / "Nothing has been asked of production for this order." — the three empty states, each pointing at where the missing thing comes from.
gotchas: A read-only desk sees live-looking buttons. Murali's and Raghav's Place hold and Release buttons are fully enabled and only refuse when pressed. If a button looks fine but keeps saying you have no permission, that is the answer, not a fault. The one thing that IS greyed out is Place hold before you have ticked a slab, and "Check stock" on a line with no design.

"Open the planning queue" no longer takes a commercial login anywhere. Production planning moved out of this module on 17 September and became the plant's own tab, and it admits only the admin login — so all four of you land on a "no access" page. The Production requests table on this screen is how the commercial desk follows the queue.

There is no Extend button, and that is deliberate, not an omission. When the days run out the slabs go back to general stock and the only way to keep them is a fresh hold with fresh days — which means re-checking that they are still there.

When a hold lapses and it was the order's last live one, the order slides backwards on its own — from Stock checked (or PI issued) back to Confirmed — and a line appears in the order's Log saying so. Nobody is told; you find out by looking. After that the PI is blocked again with "Stock check first: place a hold before issuing the PI" until new stock is held.

Expiry does not happen at midnight on a timer.
