The slabs are freed the moment somebody runs a stock check or opens finished goods, but the HOLD CARD on this screen is not refreshed by that — it can still show a green "active" chip while the countdown next to it already says "lapsed", and it will still offer you Release buttons that then refuse. Trust the countdown, not the chip. The "Held so far" column is honest either way: it stops counting a lapsed hold.

The hold card spells the consequence out rather than leaving it to be discovered: "expires 22/09/2026, 4:15 pm — on expiry the order returns to the stock check", and afterwards "lapsed 22/09/2026, 4:15 pm — the order went back to the stock check".

The Days box accepts 1 to 60. Type anything outside that — 0, 90, a word — and it is silently ignored and the standard length used instead. Nothing warns you, so check the expiry date on the hold card afterwards.
The standard five days is a setting, not a law of nature. An admin can change it, and the faint grey number in the Days box is whatever it is set to right now — read it rather than assuming five.

"Held so far" on a line is matched by design name and thickness, not by line. Two lines of the same design and thickness will both show the same combined figure, which can look like double the stock is held.

The shortfall panel compares what the line needs against what the SEARCH found, not against what you ticked. Narrow the search by grade and the shortfall figure grows accordingly — it is a fact about the yard as filtered, not about your picking.

A line with no slab count stated shows no "of X needed" in the counter and never offers a shortfall panel. There is nothing to be short of, so the screen does not nag — but it also will not warn you that you have under-picked.
Cut-to-size slabs, samples, and any slab whose mark cannot be read are simply absent from the count. So a batch you know is in the bay can legitimately show fewer slabs here than you counted by eye.
Stock not yet passed for sale is invisible to everyone except an admin. The same slabs can therefore give two different counts depending on who is looking.
Lines ticked "Sample" on the Items tab never appear in "Lines to check" — do not go hunting for them. If a line you expected is missing, check that tick box.
The confirmation line names only the first three skipped slabs and then says "…". If several were refused, open the order's Log tab, find that entry and click "details" to see the full list.

Releasing is a two-step: you have to press "Slabs" to open a hold before any release control appears. The reason box is optional but it is the only explanation anyone will ever see for why the stock went back, and it is shown on the hold card afterwards.

A slab already on a packing list shows "packed" with its tick box disabled. It cannot be released from here — it goes back through the packing list. And once every slab on a hold is packed, the hold stops being active and the release controls disappear altogether.
The order only moves to "Stock checked" if it is behind that point. Holding stock on an already-invoiced order changes nothing on the pipeline strip, by design.
entry.handsTo: Two threads leave this screen. If stock covered the order, the hold is what unlocks the proforma invoice — Setumani or Santosh moves to the Proforma tab and raises the PI, and later the same held slabs are drawn down onto a packing list, which is how a hold ends properly (it then reads "packed" rather than lapsing). If stock was short, an admin has to put the shortfall into the plant's queue for you; it goes in at the back of the whole plant's line, already carrying a first guess at the slabs, the shade and the cleaning time, which the planner then adjusts along with the batch. Its status comes back onto this same screen as Queued, Scheduled, In production and finally Produced — at which point the new slabs can be held here against the order. Meanwhile the clock is running: five days from now, if nothing has been packed and no new hold placed, the order quietly returns to the stock check and this whole screen has to be done again.

entry.title: The order checklist — the 22-point sheet, Check and Approve, and the order task list
entry.purpose: This is the internal sales order checklist: the 22-point sheet the desk works through so that nothing about a customer's order is still unknown by the time a proforma goes out and an invoice is raised. Two signatures sit on it — one person prepares it and marks it checked, a second approves — and the approval is the thing the final invoice waits for. Under it sits the order task list, the record that the outside work (container booking, CHA, BL draft, COO, CEFA, fumigation, the portal uploads, or on a domestic order the transport booking and the e-way bill) was actually done, with a date and a note.
entry.whoActs: Santosh (manager) is the only one of the four who can do everything on this screen: fill it, mark it checked, and Approve it. Setumani and Raghav can fill every box, tick every point, Save answers, Mark checked, and work the task list — their Approve button is on the screen but greyed, with the reason printed beside it. Murali can fill and mark checked, and his Approve button looks live and clickable, but pressing it comes back refused (see the refusals below). Raghav is a special case on this screen: the checklist and the task list are fully his, but the order header cards above them on the same page are not — he can type in them and press Save header, and it will be refused, so the points that are filled from the header are ones only Santosh, Setumani or Murali can actually change for him. The bay 5 dispatch team never reaches this screen at all; they have only the Dispatch Check.
steps: Open Orders, click the order number. You land on the Overview tab. There is no tab called "Checklist" — the sheet is a card near the bottom of Overview, below the receipts, headed "Internal sales order checklist".

Fill in the cards above it first — Customer purchase order, Commercial terms, Parties, Routing, Delivery/packing/contacts — and press "Save header" (a "Discard changes" button sits next to it while you have unsaved typing). The checklist fills itself in from those answers, and a green line confirms: "Saved. The checklist has been filled in again from the new answers." Several of those boxes name the point they answer — "Checklist point 9", "Checklist point 10", "Checklist point 15", and so on.

Scroll to the checklist. It is the paper sheet, point for point: 22 rows numbered 1, 1a, 1b, 1c, then 2 to 19 — PO number and date, the three kinds of evidence, description, UOM, quantity, size, rate, total value, samples, delivery schedule, Incoterms, bill-to, ship-to/notify, port of discharge, special packing, payment terms, payment mode, forwarder, receiver, customer contact.

Each row has four columns: the number, the point, a "Recorded" box holding the answer, and "Settled" — a tick box with a green "ok" or amber "open" badge. Rows still open are shaded amber and their empty box reads "Not available — ask the sender".

Type the missing answers into the Recorded boxes, or tick/untick Settled by hand. The moment anything changes, a filled-in "Save answers" button appears next to the other two. Press it. You get "Checklist saved."

Read the line under the heading: it says either "Every point is settled." or, for example, "3 points outstanding — go back to the sender for these before the PI." That sentence is the whole point of the sheet — chase the sender for those before issuing the proforma.

When the sheet is as complete as you can make it, press "Mark checked". You get "Checked.", and your name and today's date settle into the "Prepared by" box on the left. (Before anyone has pressed it, that box already shows your own name in grey with the words "you — stamped on Mark checked" — that is a preview, not a stamp.) The button then reads "Check again".

The manager (or an admin) presses "Approve". You get "Approved.", and the name and date drop into the "Approved by (Commercial Manager)" box on the right, which until then reads "not yet approved — the final invoice waits for this". The button then reads "Approve again".

Below the sheet is the "Order tasks" card. An export order is given 12 lines — Container booking, CHA, BL draft, COO (certificate of origin), CEFA, Fumigation certificate, TiO2 MOC application, RFID lock, Container pictures, Shipping documents sent to customer, Daltile portal upload, ETA sheet updated. A domestic order is given 3 — Transport booking, Transporter bills, e-Way bill.

Work each task line: tick the box when it is done (this saves immediately), then the date box beside it unlocks with today's date in it — change it if the work was actually done earlier. Type anything useful in the Note box; that saves when you click away from it. Press "Not required" on a line the customer or the shipment does not need; it moves down and shows a "not required" badge, and the button becomes "Needed after all".
The card keeps two lists — "Outstanding" at the top and "Done and not required" below, each with its own count — and prints a running sentence, e.g. "7 of 12 done, 2 not required, 3 outstanding."
Add anything this particular order needs with the "Add a task this order needs" box at the bottom and the "Add task" button. Pressing Enter in the box does the same thing.
The same Order tasks card also appears on the Documents tab, at the foot of it, which is where Raghav will usually work it, since most of the lines are his.
Everything done here is written into the Log tab. Its "Show" dropdown has a "Checklist" filter for the 22-point sheet and its approval, and a separate "Order tasks" filter for the tick list.
refusals: Approving, for Setumani and Raghav. The Approve button is visible but greyed, and hovering it and an amber line under it both say: "Only the Commercial Manager or an admin approves." Why: the sheet carries two signatures on purpose — the person who prepares it cannot also be the person who signs it off. The button is left visible rather than hidden so it is obvious the step exists and whose it is.

Approving, for Murali — this one is a trap. The Approve button appears fully enabled on his screen, with no amber line under it, but pressing it comes back with a red note: "Only the Commercial Manager or an admin approves". One half of the system was set up to let him approve (its note records the owner giving him the approval on 7 September); the test the button runs when it is pressed names only the Commercial Manager and an admin. Until that is reconciled, Murali should treat approval as Santosh's. It is worth raising rather than working around, because the two halves of the system currently disagree.

Issuing the final invoice before the sheet is approved. The Invoice tab refuses with: "The checklist must be approved before the final invoice — an admin or the Commercial Manager approves it on the order's Overview tab", and adds "A draft can be prepared meanwhile." The same refusal greys the "Invoiced" step on the pipeline strip at the top of the order, worded "The checklist must be approved before the final invoice". Once it is approved the same place reads "Checklist approved by [name] on [date] — the final invoice may be issued." Why: the invoice is the document the customer and the bank act on, so a second person confirms the order's terms before it exists.

Editing the order header, for Raghav. The header cards above the checklist look editable to him and "Save header" appears, but pressing it returns "Not available for this login." Why: his part of this module is the invoice, the checklist and the export documents — he fills the checklist on an order he does not otherwise own. The practical effect is that a point fed from the header (point 10, 15, 16, and the rest) has to be corrected by Santosh, Setumani or Murali on his behalf.

Cancelling the order, for anyone but Santosh or an admin. The red "Cancel order…" button at the top of the page is greyed with the line "Only the Commercial Manager or an admin cancels an order". Why: cancelling closes the order permanently and releases everything held against it.

Putting a date on a task that is not ticked. The date box stays greyed and hovering it says "The date is the day the task was done — tick it first"; if it is sent anyway the answer is "Only a task marked done carries a date". A line marked "not required" is in the same position — nothing was done on it, so it carries no date either. Why: a completion date on an unfinished line is the one piece of evidence on this card that would be read as a fact.
A date typed in the wrong shape: "The date must be YYYY-MM-DD".

Adding a task that is already on the list. The refusal names it: e.g. "\"Container booking\" is already on this order's task list". Capitals and stray spaces do not get round it. Why: two lines with the same name means two people ticking different copies of the same job.
Adding a task with no name: "Give the task a name" (the Add task button also stays greyed until something is typed).
If the sheet ever comes up with no rows on it at all, the card says "This order has no checklist — reload the page."
gotchas: "Mark checked" does NOT save what you have typed. If the "Save answers" button is showing, press that first. The moment the checked stamp lands, the page re-reads the order and anything still sitting unsaved in the Recorded boxes is gone.

Clearing a box the system filled in gives the answer straight back, ticked — and it happens in the same Save answers press. Every one of the 22 points is refilled from the order wherever the order has an answer for it, including delivery schedule, special packing, forwarder and receiver (those four come from the boxes of the same name in the "Delivery, packing and contacts" card) and samples (from any item line marked as a free sample on the Items tab). The right place to change point 10 or point 15 is the field in the cards above, then Save header — do not fight the checklist box.

A box you have typed something into is never overwritten — that is the other half of the same rule. The card says so under the table: "Points the order can answer are filled in automatically and refilled after every edit — an answer typed here is never overwritten." A point only keeps your typing where the order itself has nothing to say.
Un-ticking Settled by hand sticks only while the box still has text in it. Clear the box and untick it, and the next save puts the order's own answer back and ticks it again.

Points 4, 6 and 7 (Quantity, Price/Rate, Total Value) stay OPEN until some line on the order actually carries a figure. A zero is deliberately not treated as an answer, so an order whose items have no prices yet will show those three as outstanding, which is correct.
Choosing "Evidence of the order" in the header fills all three of 1a, 1b and 1c at once — the one you chose reads YES, the other two read N/A, and all three tick.

You can approve with points still open. Nothing stops it. The count beside the buttons ("3 points outstanding") is the only warning you get, and it is there so that approving an incomplete sheet is a decision rather than an accident. The Log tab records the count at the moment it was checked, e.g. "Checklist prepared and checked by Setumani · 3 points outstanding".

Approve does not require "Mark checked" first, and nothing in the system waits for "Mark checked" at all — it is the record of who prepared the sheet, nothing more. Only Approve unlocks the final invoice and the Invoiced stage.
"Check again" and "Approve again" overwrite the name and date with yours. The previous one survives only in the Log tab.
On the task card a tick saves the instant you tick it, but a note saves only when you click away from the box. Type a note and walk off with the cursor still in it and it is not saved.
Un-ticking a task clears its date — deliberately, so a line that is open again is not still carrying the day someone ticked it by mistake.
You may also empty the date box of a ticked line and leave it empty. That is allowed and means "done, day unknown" — it does not un-tick the line, and the box is yours to refill.
A task cannot be deleted, including one you added by hand. "Not required" is the way to retire a line, and "Needed after all" brings it back.

"Not required" is counted separately from "done" — the card says "7 of 12 done, 2 not required" rather than folding them together, because a fumigation certificate the buyer waived is settled work but no certificate exists.

If an order is switched from Domestic to Export (or back) after it has been opened, the new kind's task lines are added but the old kind's three or twelve are left where they are, ticks and notes intact. Mark the ones that no longer apply "Not required".

The Order tasks card is the same list on the Overview tab and on the Documents tab, but the two are separate copies on screen. A tick made on one shows on the other the next time that tab is opened, not instantly.

The log distinguishes who ticked a task from who typed a note on it. A note added later is recorded as a note, and does not credit the tick to the wrong person. A blur that changed nothing writes nothing at all.

The Documents tab shows the task card too, but the export document workbook above it only appears once the order has an export invoice on it (a draft one counts); before that the tab explains where to look instead and still shows the task list underneath.
The task card can print "This login may read this order but not change it" with every control greyed, but none of the four desks will ever see that — all four may write the checklist and its tasks.
entry.handsTo: Once Santosh (or an admin) has pressed Approve, the \"Approved by\" stamp appears on the pipeline strip at the top of the order as a green badge, and the final invoice is unblocked: Setumani or Raghav can issue it on the Invoice tab, and the order can then be moved to the Invoiced stage. Until that stamp exists only a draft invoice can be prepared. The order task list keeps running after the approval and past the invoice — Raghav works the documents lines from the Documents tab, Murali the booking and freight lines — and it closes out with the ETA sheet once the container is away. Every tick, stamp and approval on this screen is written to the Log tab under the \"Checklist\" and \"Order tasks\" filters, which is the record anyone will go back to later.

entry.title: Proforma invoice (PI) — the Proforma tab on an order
entry.purpose: This is where the priced offer the customer pays against is produced. You take the order as it stands, freeze it into a numbered proforma invoice, add the few shipping and banking facts the order itself does not hold, then issue it. The issued PI is the paper the customer holds: it names the amount, the account to pay into and the goods, and once issued it never changes again. If the deal moves you do not edit it — you issue a replacement under a new number and the old one is struck out.
entry.whoActs: Santosh (manager) and Setumani (executive) do everything here: build the draft, edit it, issue, record acceptance, revise. Only Santosh (or an admin) can cancel a PI by hand — Setumani cannot, and her Cancel button is greyed with its own reason beside it. Raghav and Murali can open this tab and see every PI, open every PDF and read every detail, but Create draft, Edit draft, Issue, Customer accepted, Revise and Cancel are all dead for them; the tab is reading only for those two desks. The reason is not repeated on every button — one short grey sentence sits at the end of each PI's row of buttons, and one under the Create draft button at the top. Raghav and Murali will see two sentences on a PI: the one saying proformas are not their desk, and the one saying cancelling is the manager's. The bay 5 dispatch team never reaches an order at all, so they never see this screen. Nobody's buttons are hidden — a desk that cannot act still sees the button, greyed, with the sentence saying why.
steps: Open the order and go to the Proforma tab. Everything this order has ever had is listed here — the live PI, any drafts, and the cancelled ones a revision replaced. Newest number first, except that a cancelled PI sits directly under the PI that replaced it, struck through, with its reason and the number that replaced it beside it, so nothing ever disappears from the list.

Read each PI's card at a glance: the number (struck through if it is cancelled), a one-word status — draft, issued, accepted or cancelled — whether it is EXPORT or DOMESTIC, the PI's own printed date, then the dates it was issued, is valid until, was accepted and was cancelled, and 'Revises <number>' where it replaces an earlier one. On the right: the total, the slab count and how many lines it has.

Read the amber banners at the top before doing anything. 'This order has no items — a PI built now would print an empty table.' and 'No consignee on the order and no client address to fall back on — the PI would print a blank consignee.' are warnings, not blocks: you can still build a draft, but the customer will get a page with a hole in it. Go back and fix the order first. A third amber banner — 'Stock check first: a PI is issued only once a hold is placed on this order and still live.' — appears only once a draft exists on the order, and it is telling you in advance that Issue will be refused.

Read the grey line beside the Create draft button. It repeats that each PI takes its own number and the order keeps its own, names the PI that is currently live, and says whether a PI expires. It also reminds you the advance is asked for on the PI but recorded as a receipt on the order, not here.

Press 'Create draft from this order'. This freezes the order's parties, its lines, its quantities and its rates onto a brand-new proforma number — not the order number. The salesperson and the selling company are copied off the order at this moment too, and so are the delivery and payment terms and the ports. The PI's own printed date is set to today; there is no field to change it. The screen confirms: 'Draft PI built from the order, under its own number.'

Press 'Edit draft' on the new draft to fill in what the order does not hold. Eight boxes: which bank account prints (Kotak on export, ICICI on domestic by default), which GST registration it goes out under, the delivery date, a discount in the PI's currency, gross weight, net weight, the salesperson's name, and the Terms & Conditions box. Gross and net are free text — type them as you want them printed, for example '24,500 KGS'; nothing works them out for you. Press 'Save draft' to keep the changes, 'Discard changes' to close the panel and throw away what you have typed since the last save, or 'Edit draft' again (it now reads 'Stop editing') to do the same.

Type the Terms and Conditions yourself. The box prints exactly what you type and nothing else — no container size, no tonnage, no weight is ever put in it for you. Left blank, the PI prints a labelled empty box, which is a correct document.

Press 'Show detail' on any PI to see what was actually frozen: consignee, notify party, delivery and payment terms, ports, gross and net, the selling company, the bank, the GST number, the validity, the salesperson, then the full printed line table — item code, description, thickness, slabs, HSN, unit, quantity, rate and amount — with the discount row, the total and the amount in words. 'Hide detail' closes it again. Opening the edit panel opens this detail too.

Press 'Open PDF' at any time. It opens in a new tab and is rendered fresh by the system from the frozen record — what you see is exactly what the customer gets. Everyone on the desk can do this, including the read-only desks.

Press 'Issue' when the draft is right. The PI goes live, gets its issue date, and the order moves to the 'PI issued' stage. At this moment the bank details and the GST registration behind your chosen boxes are re-read from Settings — so an account number an admin corrected while the draft sat gets onto the paper. Your choices themselves are not changed. After issue nothing about the PI ever re-freezes again. If issuing retired an older PI, the confirmation says so: '<number> issued — <old number> is cancelled as revised.'

When the customer confirms, press 'Customer accepted' on the issued PI. This stamps the acceptance date and writes it to the order's log. It does not move the order to another stage — acceptance is evidence, not a step — and it does not record any money.

If the deal changes after issue, press 'Revise (new number)'. A box asks why. Type a reason: it is not compulsory here, but it is the only explanation the order's log will carry for why a second number was taken. You get a fresh draft on a NEW number, built from the order as it now stands, carrying over the shipping facts and the bank and GST choices you typed on the old one. Edit it and issue it. The moment you issue it, the old PI is cancelled as 'Revised as <new number>' — not before.

If a PI has to be withdrawn without a replacement — or a draft was built by mistake — Santosh presses 'Cancel'. A box asks why and the reason is compulsory. The number stays in the register for ever, struck through, with your reason printed beside it.
refusals: 'Your login reads proforma invoices — the Commercial Executive or Manager builds and issues them' — what Raghav and Murali see on every PI here, and under the Create draft button. Both of them write on their own screens, so their general permission alone cannot tell the system that proformas are not theirs; this sentence is the specific answer. The reason: the PI is the priced commitment to the customer, and the desk that negotiated the price is the desk that issues it.
'Your login can read this order but not write to it' — shown instead of the above when a login cannot write anywhere in the module. Same effect: look, don't touch.

'Only the Commercial Manager or an admin cancels a PI' — beside a greyed Cancel button for everyone else, Setumani included. Cancelling destroys a commitment the customer may already be holding, so it is kept one rank above the person who issued it.

'Stock check first: place a hold before issuing the PI' — refused when you press Issue without a live hold on the order. The screen warns in advance with an amber banner as soon as a draft exists. The reason: a PI promises specific material on a date. Without slabs actually held, you are promising stock that someone else's order can take tomorrow.

'The PI has no lines — add items to the order and rebuild the draft' — refused when you try to issue a draft with an empty table. An empty proforma is not a document; it is a blank page with our letterhead on it.

'Only a draft can be issued (this PI is issued)' / 'Only a draft can be edited (this PI is accepted)' / 'Only an issued PI can be accepted (this PI is draft)' / 'Only an issued or accepted PI can be revised (this PI is cancelled)' — the same idea each time: once a PI has left the building it is the customer's paper, and the only way to change it is a fresh numbered document.

'A draft revising this PI already exists (SAL-ORD/26-27/N0043) — edit and issue that one' — and on screen the Revise button is replaced by the line 'Revision <number> in draft — issue it to retire this PI'. Two people revising the same PI would burn two numbers and leave two drafts racing to replace one paper, so only one revision may be in flight.

'Cancelling a PI needs a reason — the register prints it beside the cancelled number' — a blank reason is refused. The number stays on the books for ever; a struck-through number nobody can account for years later is worse than no record at all.
'A cancelled PI cannot be cancelled' (and the same wording for an old superseded one) — you cannot cancel twice, and the status is checked before the reason is even asked for.

'A proforma numbered SAL-ORD/26-27/N0044 already exists — check the counter in Settings' — the counter has been set back or overridden by hand and is about to reissue a number. Two documents with one number is the one thing a numbered register cannot survive. Settings is the admin's screen, so this one goes to the admin, not to you.

'A cancelled order cannot move' (or 'A closed order cannot move') — issuing a PI on an order that has already been cancelled or closed is refused, because issuing moves the order forward and a finished order does not move. Note that building a draft on such an order is NOT refused — only issuing it is.
gotchas: A greyed button is an answer, not a fault. Every refused action stays on screen with the reason written at the end of that PI's row of buttons. If Raghav asks why Issue is grey, the sentence beside it already says so.

There is no way to delete a draft. A draft you no longer want has to be CANCELLED, which only Santosh or an admin can do — and the number it took is gone either way. So do not build drafts casually to look at them.

The lines, prices and parties are frozen the second you press 'Create draft'. Editing the order afterwards does NOT update an existing draft. To get the new items or the new price onto a PI, build a fresh draft from the order, or revise the issued one.

Only eight things are editable on a draft, and none of them is a price. Delivery date, discount, gross weight, net weight, salesperson, the terms box, the bank and the GST registration. Everything else — the parties, the lines, the rates, the delivery and payment terms, the ports — comes from the order and can only be changed by editing the order and building a fresh draft.
The PI number is not the order number, and a revision is not 'version 2'. Each PI takes its own number from the proforma counter. The order keeps one number for life.
Numbers are never reused, and a failed draft leaves a gap in the series. That gap is deliberate and correct — a number handed out once is gone.

'Revise' does not retire the old PI. The old one stays live, and the customer's copy stays valid, until you actually ISSUE the replacement. Both things happen in the same instant. So an abandoned revision draft leaves the original standing, which is the intended behaviour.

A revision does NOT carry over the salesperson name or the selling company you see on the old PI. Those are read off the order again, so if the order was reassigned in the meantime the new PI carries the new name and the new company. The delivery date, discount, weights, terms box and the bank and GST choices DO carry over.

Issuing ANY draft retires every other live PI on that order — even a draft you built from scratch rather than through Revise. The customer holds exactly one live PI at a time. Build a second draft 'just to compare' and issuing it will kill the first.

Bank and GST details are re-read from Settings at the moment of issue, not at the moment of drafting. If a draft sits for a week and an admin corrects an account number in the meantime, the corrected number goes on the paper. Your CHOICE of account is not changed, only the details behind it.

The bank and GST boxes are greyed on a PI sold by Monolith, the US company. The hint explains it: that company has one account of its own and is not an Indian exporter, so no GST number, RBI code, customs office or Indian-origin declaration prints on it at all. The greyed boxes say so plainly — the GST box reads 'None — this PI prints no GSTIN' and the bank box names Monolith's own account.
A Monolith PI takes its number from Monolith's own series, not Pacific's, so its numbers will not run on from the last Pacific PI you issued. That is correct, not a counter fault.

The salesperson name prints on domestic PIs only. On an export PI it is kept on the record but never printed, and the detail panel says so in brackets. The hint under the box tells you before you type.
There is no vessel box. The proforma stopped printing a vessel in September 2026 by the owner's instruction. The vessel is recorded on the invoice, which is where the packing list reads it from.

A stock hold lapses after five days (the admin can set anything from one to sixty). An order can show 'stock checked' and still be refused at Issue, because the hold behind that tick has expired. Place a fresh hold.
Revise and Cancel ask for their reason in the browser's own small pop-up box. Pressing Cancel in that pop-up abandons the whole action silently — nothing happens and no message appears.

Right now a PI never expires. The line at the top of the tab says 'A PI does not expire' because the validity setting is zero. If an admin sets a number of days, the same line will start saying how many and the PDF will print a validity date.
'Customer accepted' records nothing about money. The advance the PI asks for is recorded separately as a receipt on the order. Marking a PI accepted does not mean it has been paid.
Cancelled PIs never leave the list, and they sort under the PI that replaced them rather than by date — so the retired number is read right beside the number that retired it.
A blank discount box means zero, not 'leave it as it was'. A negative figure is treated as zero too, and the amount in words is rewritten whenever the discount changes.
entry.handsTo: Issuing the PI moves the order to the 'PI issued' stage and puts it in front of the customer. Two things then happen elsewhere: the customer pays the advance the PI asked for, which Santosh or Setumani record as a receipt on the order's own screen (not here — this tab records no money), and once material is packed the order goes on to the packing list. Later, Raghav raises the final commercial invoice, and that invoice looks at the live PI to decide which of our accounts to print, so the bank you chose on this PI follows the order all the way to the invoice. If the live PI is ever cancelled without a replacement, the invoice loses that inheritance and falls back to the default for the order's type — ICICI on domestic, Kotak on export.

entry.title: Packing lists — what goes in each crate, and the moment the stone stops being ours to sell
entry.purpose: This is where a confirmed order turns into a real shipment: which slabs (and which cut-to-size pieces) go in which crate, their measured sizes and the customer's own numbering, the container and seal details, and the two printed sheets the container is stuffed from and customs reads. It is also the screen that moves stock — sending a list for the dispatch check takes those slabs off the shelf so nobody else can sell them, and marking the list dispatched takes them out of finished goods altogether.
entry.whoActs: Santosh and Setumani are the two people who can actually build and move a packing list — add crates, add slabs, type measurements, send it for the check, finalise it, mark it dispatched. They are also the only two who get the "Open the check" link on a list that is with bay 5 or has already been passed, which takes them onto bay 5's own screen. Raghav and Murali can open the register and every list and print both PDFs, but nothing they do here will save: they are readers on this screen. Bay 5 never reaches this screen at all — a dispatch-team login that types the address lands on the Dispatch Check instead, which is the only tab they have. Beware: Raghav's and Murali's buttons here are NOT greyed out. Every control looks live to them and only answers "Not available for this login." when they press it. That is how the whole Commercial module behaves for a reader, not a quirk of this screen, so the same warning applies on the order's own Packing tab, where the button to start a list also looks live to them.
steps: Start the list from the ORDER, not from this screen. Open the order, go to its Packing tab, and choose either 'From a hold' (pack what was already reserved for this order on the Stock tab) or 'By slab numbers' (type them — commas, spaces and ranges like 150905-150910 all work; it tells you how many it recognised). Press Create. Any slab it will not accept is named with the reason; the rest go on and the list opens as a Draft. If the order already has a list, that whole card is replaced by one sentence telling you which list it is — there is nothing to press.

On the packing-lists register, use the stage chips across the top — All, Draft, Awaiting check, Verified, Rejected, Final, Dispatched — or the search box (list number, order, client or container). Click a list number to open it. A list waiting for bay 5 also shows how many lines are still to check. Fifty lists to a page, with Previous and Next at the foot.

At the top of the list you get the order, client, Export or Domestic, who started it and when, plus running counts: Slabs, Cut pieces (only once the list has cut-to-size lines), Packages, Sqm, how many slabs are not in a crate yet, and Checked. Read Checked as 'passed out of everything on the list' — 12/14 with '2 unfit' underneath is two refusals, not two still to look at.

Build the crates first. Under 'Crates', press + Wooden Crate, + Sample Box or + Bundle. Each crate gets the next number automatically and you can type over it. Fill gross kg, net kg and the crate's own L / W / H — those three are always in centimetres, whatever unit the slab sizes are in — plus any remark. Remove takes a crate off. A running line underneath shows what the printed sheet will say for each design and thickness.

Put slabs in crates. In the Slabs table pick a crate from the dropdown on each row, or tick several rows at once — a blue bar appears saying '8 selected' with a crate picker, Assign, Unassign and Clear. The 'Unassigned' count at the top tells you what is still loose. Remove at the end of a row takes the slab off the list altogether.

Type what was actually measured. For each slab fill the customer's own slab number and batch number (these print on the measurement sheet), and the measured Length and Width. Sqm works itself out. Use the 'Sizes in cm / in' switch beside the Slabs heading to choose which unit you type and print in — the stone does not change, only the way it is written. The length and width boxes are NOT blank when a slab arrives: they are pre-filled with the nominal size on file converted across, which is 348 × 201 cm on almost every slab. A row nobody has measured therefore looks measured, so work through the whole table.
Add more slabs later if needed, from the 'Add slabs' box at the foot of the table: type numbers, or pick one of the order's live holds from the dropdown (it shows how many slabs each hold still has).

If this shipment is cut-to-size work, use the Cut to size table instead of (or as well as) the slabs. On a brand-new empty list a card asks 'What does this list pack?' with two buttons, Slabs or Cut-to-size pieces. Once one kind is on the list, a button at the very bottom of the screen offers the other — '+ Add slabs to this list' or '+ Add cut-to-size pieces'. The cut-to-size line takes crate no., drawing no., piece no., design/material, L / W / thickness, sqft, quantity, building/area and weight, with a subtotal per crate and a TOTAL row. Leave Sqft blank and it is worked out from the size and the quantity. The crate, drawing and building carry down to the next line so a whole crate is quick to type.

Fill the Container & weights panel when the container is booked: Container No., E-Seal No., Liner's OTL No., Vehicle No., gross and net weight, the Packages wording and any notes. This panel has its own 'Save header' button — the tables save as you go, but this one does not save until you press it.
Press 'Send for dispatch check'. This is the point of no return for the contents: the slabs go to packed in finished goods so nobody else can sell them, and the list goes to bay 5.

Wait for bay 5. They pass the list (Verified) or refuse it (Rejected, with their note in a coloured band at the top of the screen). If you sent it too early, 'Reopen' pulls it back and hands every slab back to stock.
On a verified list press 'Finalise'. That makes it the document the container is stuffed from and locks the contents for good.

When the container has actually left, press 'Mark dispatched'. The slabs leave finished goods under this order and client name, the holds that reserved them are closed off, and the order moves to Dispatched.

Print at any stage: 'Packing list PDF' and 'Measurement list PDF' at the top of the list, or the PL / Measmt links on each row of the register. Anyone who can see the screen can print them, readers included.
refusals: A second packing list on the same order is refused: 'This order already has packing list PL/26-27/0041 (draft) — one PI has one packing list. Add crates and slabs to it, or reopen it if it was sent too early.' One proforma invoice means one shipment; two lists on one order would mean two shipments billed as one. A rejected list is the one exception — it is meant to be reopened rather than replaced, so it does not block a fresh start. On the order's Packing tab this arrives as a plain sentence where the Create card would be, not as a red error.

A slab that is not free to pack is refused by name, with the reason beside it: 'already on this list', 'not found in finished goods', 'marked CTS — not a full slab', 'RETURNED — release it back to available in finished goods first', 'held under ORD-…' (somebody else's reference), 'already PACKED'. The others still go on. The packing list is the document the container is stuffed from, so a list claiming a slab that is not in the crate is worse than a short list. If nothing at all can be packed you get 'No slab could be packed: #150903 (already PACKED); …'.

Changing crates, slabs or cut-to-size lines after the list has gone to bay 5 is refused: 'PL/26-27/0041 is awaiting check — reopen it before changing what is packed.' The dispatch team is standing in front of the crates reading that sheet; it must not change under them. On the screen the boxes simply go flat and uneditable and the Add and Remove buttons disappear, so you will normally meet this sentence only if somebody else sent the list while you had it open.

The cm/in switch goes dead once the list has left Commercial, and hovering it says 'The unit can only be switched while the list is with Commercial'. Press it anyway (two people, one list) and the answer is 'PL/26-27/0041 is awaiting check — the unit can only be switched while the list is with Commercial.' Same reason — the sheet in bay 5's hands must not turn into inches halfway through the check.

'Send for dispatch check' is greyed with the reason on hover when there is nothing to send: 'Add at least one slab or cut-to-size line before submitting.' That is the only hover reason you will ever see on it, because the button is simply not drawn on a list that is past Draft or Rejected.

Sending can quietly shorten the list, and it tells you: 'Sent for the dispatch check — 2 slab(s) dropped: #150907 (already PACKED on PL/26-27/0038); #150912 (not found in finished goods).' Those slabs were taken by something else between building and sending — the named list is the one that got there first. If nothing at all survives, nothing moves and you get 'No slab on PL/26-27/0041 could be packed.'

Taking a slab off a list that has already been sent once is refused when stock will not take it back: 'Slab #150903 is still PACKED in finished goods (…) — it stays on PL/26-27/0041 until it can be put back.' The row on the list is the only thing pointing at that slab; delete it and the slab is packed against nothing and effectively lost. On a list that has never been sent, Remove always works.

Reopen tells you the same thing rather than refusing: 'Reopened; 14 slab(s) back in stock. 1 slab(s) are still PACKED in finished goods: #150903 (the inventory did not confirm the release).' Anything named there has to be chased in finished goods by hand — nothing else in the module will mention it again.
Two crates with the same number: 'Crate 3 is already on PL/26-27/0041.' And 'A crate number starts at 1.' The crate number is what is stencilled on the box and printed on the marks.

'Finalise', 'Reopen' and 'Mark dispatched' are each drawn only at the moment they apply — Finalise on a verified list, Reopen on one that is with bay 5 or came back rejected, Mark dispatched on a final one. If the list moved under you the sentences are: 'PL/26-27/0041 is awaiting check — only a verified list can be finalised'; 'PL/26-27/0041 is final — only a submitted or rejected list can be reopened'; 'PL/26-27/0041 is verified — finalise it before dispatch.' Only bay 5's pass turns a draft into the stuffing document, and once the check has passed the way back is a swap, not a rebuild.

Dispatch with anything the floor refused or never looked at: 'PL/26-27/0041 was not dispatched. Nothing ships until the list is corrected. 2 slab(s) marked unfit by the dispatch check: #150903 (Chipped edge); #150911 (Crack) — swap each one for a slab of the same design and thickness. 1 slab(s) not yet checked: #150920 — the dispatch team has to pass them first. 1 cut-to-size line(s) marked unfit: Crate 4 / piece 12 (Size short) — each one has to be recut and repacked.' A packing list cannot be split and a final list's contents cannot be edited, so the honest answer is 'not this list, not yet' with every offending line named. A refused slab is swapped; a refused cut piece is recut, because there is no shelf of other people's kitchen worktops to take a replacement from.

Dispatch before the money: 'PL/26-27/0041 was not dispatched. The advance is short: USD 5,000.00 of the USD 20,000.00 asked (30% of USD 66,666.67). Record it against order ORD-… — the truck does not leave before the advance.' This is the only place in the whole module where payment is asked about — packing, the check and finalising are all free of it — so it is deliberately the last gate. Only Santosh can waive it, and only with a reason in writing, on the order: 'Only the Commercial Manager or an admin waives the advance.'

Dispatch when a slab has changed underneath you: 'PL/26-27/0041 was not dispatched — 1 of 14 slab(s) cannot leave: #150903 (marked CTS — cut to size, not dispatchable as a full slab). Nothing has moved; fix the slab or take it off the list, then dispatch again.' It checks every slab BEFORE moving any, so a refusal costs nothing and leaves nothing half done. In the rarer case where something changed mid-dispatch: 'PL/26-27/0041 is not marked dispatched — 11 of 14 slab(s) went out and 3 were refused: … Check those slabs in finished goods before trying again.' And a list carrying no slabs at all is simply told 'PL/26-27/0041 has no slabs'.

Swap is refused where it does not belong: 'A draft list has no slab to swap — swapping is for a verified or final list whose slab the dispatch check refused'; 'Slab #150903 has not been marked unfit — only a refused slab is swapped'; 'Slab #150950 cannot replace #150903: 2 cm, not 3 cm'; 'Slab #150950 is already on PL/26-27/0041.' A swap is like-for-like that the customer never sees on the invoice — a different colour or a 2 cm for a 3 cm is a new order line, not a swap.

Typing into a size box: on the slab table a bad figure answers 'Length must be a number of cm' (or 'of in', whichever the list is set to), and the same for width. On a cut-to-size line it names what you typed: 'Length must be a number of cm — "1030 mm" is not', and likewise for width and thickness; sqft and weight say 'Sqft must be a number — "abc" is not' with no unit. A commercial comma in a figure is read as a thousands separator, not a mistake. A size box that was typed but could not be read used to save as blank, which printed an empty size, an empty sqft, and a sheet TOTAL short by that line's whole area — on a customs document.

A cut-to-size line with no material: 'Name the design — a line with no material names nothing that can be packed.' A silly quantity is caught on the screen first — 'Quantity is a whole number of pieces, 1 to 10000' — and if it gets past that, 'Quantity looks wrong — 36000 pieces on one line. Split it, or check the decimal point.'

Small ones worth recognising when adding slabs: 'Name the slabs to add' (the box was empty), 'That hold has no slabs still held' (everything on it has been released or packed already), 'That hold does not belong to this order', and 'That crate is not on this list' if a crate is deleted while you are assigning to it.

Raghav and Murali: every write here answers 'Not available for this login.' Packing is Setumani's and Santosh's to write; Raghav needs the finished list to raise the invoice and Murali needs the container and weight figures to book freight, so both can read it and print it, and neither can change what is in a crate.
gotchas: Raghav's and Murali's controls are NOT greyed out on this screen. Add buttons, editable cells, Send for dispatch check — all of it looks live and only refuses when pressed, with 'Not available for this login.' That is true across the module, not just here, so the same trap waits on the order's Packing tab. If either of them needs something changed, Setumani or Santosh has to do it.

The tables save themselves; the header does not. Every box in Crates, Slabs and Cut to size saves the moment you leave it or press Enter — tabbing out of a box you changed does save it, tabbing through boxes you did not touch writes nothing, and there is no Save button. But the Container & weights panel has its own 'Save header' button, and typing there and walking away loses the typing.

The measured sizes are pre-filled, not blank. Every slab arrives carrying the nominal size on file converted into centimetres, which is 348 × 201 on almost every slab in the yard, and the Sqm on both sheets is worked out from whatever is in those boxes. A slab nobody put a tape to therefore prints a plausible, wrong figure rather than an obviously empty one.

Sending for the dispatch check is the moment the stone stops being available to anyone else. Before that, two draft lists on two different orders can both hold the same slab; the first one sent wins it, and the second is told so by name — and told which list took it — when it sends.

Reopening undoes all of that: every slab goes back to available in stock AND every verdict on the list is wiped, slabs and cut lines alike. That is deliberate — a list about to change is not a list bay 5 has checked — but it does mean the floor has to check the whole thing again.

Reopening does not clear bay 5's written note, and worse, it changes colour. The rejection wording stays at the top of the screen and, because the list is a draft again, it is now shown in a green band instead of a red one. Read the words, not the colour.

A rejected list is a trap here. You can edit it and press 'Send for dispatch check' straight away without reopening — and every mark from the last check stays on it. The slabs that passed are still ticked as passed, so bay 5's screen can offer 'Verify — all fit' the moment it arrives, over stone nobody has looked at since you changed it; and any cut-to-size line they refused is still refused, which will block the dispatch. Their 'mark the crate correct' shortcut only touches lines nobody has looked at yet, so it will not clear a stale refusal either. If a list came back rejected, Reopen it first, then rebuild.

A list carrying only cut-to-size lines and no slabs cannot be sent for the check or dispatched at all: it answers 'No slab on PL/26-27/0041 could be packed', and 'PL/26-27/0041 has no slabs'. In practice every list that has to move needs at least one slab on it. Worth raising before a pure cut-to-size shipment is planned this way.

Contents lock at the check but the paperwork does not. Container number, seal, liner OTL, vehicle, gross and net weight, the Packages wording and the notes stay editable right through Verified and Final, up until the list is marked dispatched — because those are known at stuffing time, which is after the check.
Removing a crate does not remove its slabs. They drop back to unassigned so you can put them in another box. A slab is a real thing; a crate is just how you chose to group them this morning.

The Packages line ('07 Wooden Crate(S) + 08 Sample Box') writes itself from the crates and keeps itself true as crates come and go — unless somebody typed their own wording, which is never overwritten. Blanking the box refills it from the crates rather than leaving it empty, because the invoice reads that line.

The cm/in switch is only a lens. The measurement is stored one way underneath and only the way it reads changes, so flipping it mid-list never alters a figure already typed. Crate L / W / H are always centimetres and ignore the switch entirely. Cut-to-size lines are stored in millimetres regardless, and converted the same way on screen and on both sheets.

Swap only appears in two places at once: the list must be verified or final, and the slab must be one bay 5 marked unfit. It offers only slabs of the same design and thickness that are available or already held for this order (the first 150 — type a batch or number to narrow it), and the replacement goes in unchecked, so the floor must pass it before the container can go.
Dispatch is all or nothing. There is no half-dispatched packing list — one slab that cannot leave stops the whole container, and you either fix that slab or rebuild the list.

The numbers on the stage chips at the top of the register are the totals for the whole module and do not respond to the search box. Type a client name and the rows below narrow while the chips stay where they were.

The 'Vessel / Flight No.' box on the printed packing list only fills once an invoice exists for this order and someone has put a vessel on it; the B/L and S/B boxes always print empty, there is nowhere in the module that holds them. The measurement sheet's reference box reads 'Not yet invoiced' until there is one.

Crate, piece and edge labels are NOT printed from here — they come off the Articles screen, which asks this list for its crates. If a customer's article codes are unresolved, the barcode labels refuse to print even though the packing list itself is fine.

A cut-to-size line is checked by the floor line by line, exactly as a slab is, and the 'Checked' figure at the top counts both kinds. If something is refused after the list was already passed, an amber band appears at the top of this screen naming it — that band is the only place Commercial is told, because nobody from this desk sits on the check screen.
entry.handsTo: Pressing 'Send for dispatch check' hands the list to bay 5's Dispatch Check screen, and the order moves to Packing. Bay 5 walks the crates and marks each slab and each cut-to-size line fit or unfit, line by line or a whole crate at a time; they either verify the list or reject it with a note, and either way the answer lands back on this screen in a coloured band at the top. Verifying carries the order through Dispatch check to Ready on the spot; rejecting pulls it back to Packing, sends the refused slabs back to stock and takes them off the list, while a refused cut-to-size line stays on the list with the fault written on it. From there it comes back to Setumani or Santosh: rejected means reopen and rebuild (or swap the refused slabs), verified means Finalise, which locks the contents and makes this the document the container is stuffed from. Once the container has actually left, 'Mark dispatched' takes the slabs out of finished goods under the order and the client's name, closes off the holds that reserved them, and moves the order to Dispatched. From the finished list, Raghav raises the commercial invoice and the delivery challan off these crates, weights and measurements, and takes the same figures into the export documents he does outside this system; Murali reads the container, seal and weight figures for the freight booking; and the Articles screen prints crate, piece and edge labels off this list's crates.

entry.title: Dispatch check (bay 5) — checking the crates before the container is stuffed
entry.purpose: This is the last physical look at a shipment before it leaves. Commercial hands over a packing list and the dispatch team walks the crates, saying line by line whether each slab and each cut-to-size piece is fit to ship. A list that passes goes back to Commercial as ready; a list that fails goes back as work to redo. It is also where a slab found cracked while the container is being loaded gets flagged, which stops the truck until it is put right.
entry.whoActs:
Three desks can act here, and two desks cannot see this screen at all — which is unusual, because everywhere else in Commercial a read-only desk still sees the page with the buttons greyed out. Here it is all or nothing.

ACT: the bay 5 dispatch team (this is their only screen — they sign in and land straight on it, and the side menu has exactly one row, "Dispatch Check", and nothing else), Santosh (manager), and Setumani (executive).

CANNOT SEE IT: Raghav (documents) and Murali (logistics). For them this screen does not exist — there is no row for it in their menu, and if they are sent the link they get a "no access" page. Nothing is greyed; the door simply isn't there.

ONE BUTTON IS COMMERCIAL'S ALONE: the "Swap" button, which appears beside a refused slab on a verified or final list. Santosh and Setumani see it. The bay 5 team does not see it at all — deliberately, so nobody in the bay taps a button that is only going to refuse them. Picking a replacement slab is Commercial's decision, not the checker's.

ONE MORE THING BAY 5 CANNOT DO: reopen a list. That is Santosh's or Setumani's, from the packing list itself, and it is not on this screen.

WHAT THE BAY 5 TEAM DELIBERATELY CANNOT SEE, even on a list they are checking: prices, rates, amounts, the customer's tax registrations, the billing address and the payment terms. The screen shows the order number and the customer name and nothing more about the order. Bay 5 also cannot see any packing list that Commercial is still building, or one that has already gone — only the four states below.
steps: Open the screen. The bay 5 login lands here automatically. Four tabs run across the top, each with a live count: **To check** (lists waiting), **At loading** (lists already passed that are now being stuffed into the container), **Verified**, and **Rejected**. A **Refresh** button sits on the right — the queue does not update itself, so tap it when you come back to the tablet.

Pick a list off the queue. "To check" is sorted oldest first on purpose: the container that has been waiting longest is holding up a shipment, so it is at the top. The other three tabs are the other way round, newest first, because you are looking back at what was just done. Each row shows the packing list number, the order number, the customer, whether it is Export or Domestic, the package summary, the container and vehicle number if known, and how long it has been waiting ("40 min ago", "3 h ago", "2 days ago"). The big number on the right is how many lines you have to check — slabs and cut-to-size pieces added together — with the split written underneath. On the "To check" tab every row also carries a running tally, "12 fit · 1 unfit · 6 to do"; on an untouched list that reads "0 fit". On the "At loading" tab a list that has picked up a late finding says so on the row: "3 unfit — awaiting a swap".

Tap the row to open "Check the crates". The top card repeats the list number and status, the order and customer, the packages, container, seal and vehicle number, and tells you which unit the sizes are printed in ("sizes in cm" or in inches). "Back to the queue" is top right. On a list that has already been concluded, the note Commercial was sent sits in a coloured box here — green on a verified list, red on a rejected one — so you can read what was reported without asking.
Read the progress bar. Under the header it says "14 fit · 1 unfit · 6 still to check" and "15 of 21", with a bar filling as you go. This is the number that decides whether you are allowed to finish.

Work crate by crate. The lines are grouped under headings that also carry the count — "Crate 3 · Wooden Crate · 480 kg net · 6 slab(s) · 2 cut-to-size line(s)" — and slabs and cut-to-size pieces in the same crate are shown together, because that is how they are stacked in front of you. Three other headings can appear: "Crate 7 · as printed on the cut-to-size sheet" (a crate number the customer's drawing sheet uses that isn't one of our crate records), "A crate that is no longer on this list", and "Not in a crate".

Check a slab. Each slab row shows the customer's slab number in large type with ours in brackets — "A-114 (ours 158138)". Where the customer has no number of their own, you get our number on its own. Under it: the design or the customer's product code, the thickness, the grade, the batch, the size and the square metres.

Check a cut-to-size piece. Each piece row shows "Piece 14" (and "× 3 pcs" if it is a multiple), the design, the finished size, the drawing number — or "No drawing number" where there isn't one — the room it is for, the square feet, the weight, and any note typed on it. A cut-to-size list has no slabs on it at all — it still has to be checked piece by piece.

Tap **Fit** or **Unfit** on each line. Both are big thumb-sized buttons. A line you mark Fit turns green; Unfit turns red. Fit saves on the one tap — no reason, no confirmation — so tap it on the line you are actually looking at.

If you tap Unfit, say what is wrong. A panel opens asking "What is wrong with it?" with eight ready-made buttons: **Chipped edge, Crack, Scratch, Stain / mark, Wrong design, Wrong thickness, Size short, Not in crate**. If none of them fits there is a **Something else** box you can type into, then **Mark unfit**. **Cancel** backs out, and tapping Unfit again closes the panel. One tap on a reason records the verdict — there is no separate save.
To go faster on a crate that is clean, use **Mark crate as correct — 12 line(s)** on the crate heading. It marks only the lines nobody has looked at yet, under that heading and nowhere else.

To pass a whole clean list, use **Mark all as correct — 38 line(s)** at the top. It asks you to confirm first, and underneath it says in words what it will do: "Marks every line nobody has looked at yet. Lines already marked unfit are left exactly as they are." Both shortcuts report back exactly what they did: "38 marked correct, 2 left unfit".
Type a note if Commercial should know something — the box is labelled "Note (optional)", "Anything Commercial should know". Optional. It only appears on a list you are checking for the first time.

Finish with the one big button at the bottom of the header card. It reads **Verify — all fit** in green if every line passed, or turns red and reads **Reject — 3 unfit** if anything failed. Same button, and it tells you which outcome you are about to cause before you tap it.

AT THE LOADING BAY (a list on the "At loading" or "Verified" tab): there is no Verify button any more and no note box — the check is over. But every line still has Fit and Unfit on it, so a slab that turns out cracked while the container is being stuffed can be marked here where you are standing. Nothing is unpacked and the list keeps its status; what changes is that the shipment is now blocked until Commercial puts it right. A band across the top of the card tells you where the list stands: "3 line(s) refused at loading — nothing ships until each slab is swapped for one of the same design and thickness, and each cut-to-size line is recut", or "1 line(s) still to check — nothing ships until they are marked fit", or, when there is nothing outstanding, "This list has been checked. A line found unfit while the container is being loaded can still be marked here; the truck does not leave until it is put right."
refusals: **You cannot finish while any line is unmarked.** The big Verify/Reject button stays greyed and hovering it says "3 line(s) still to check", with "Every line has to be marked before the list can be finished." printed underneath. If it is somehow sent anyway the answer names which kind is outstanding — "2 slab(s) and 1 cut-to-size line(s) have not been checked yet" — rather than just a number, so you are not sent hunting through slabs you have already done. WHY: a list is verified because every line was looked at, not because somebody scrolled to the bottom of the screen.

**An Unfit with no reason is refused: "Say what is wrong with it".** The Mark unfit button stays dead until you pick a reason or type one. WHY: an unfit line sends the whole list back and pulls the order back to Packing. "No reason given" is not something Commercial can act on at eight in the evening with a container booked.

**"Mark all as correct" and "Mark crate as correct" never clear an unfit line.** The confirmation says so in words: "Mark all 38 unchecked line(s) on PL-0142 correct? Anything already marked unfit is left exactly as it is." And the answer always names what it skipped: "38 marked correct, 2 left unfit". Even if somebody marks a line unfit on another tablet in the split second while your bulk action is in flight, that finding survives and is counted as skipped. WHY: losing a deliberate finding silently is the one failure this whole screen exists to prevent — a bulk action that reported only its successes would let you walk away believing the crate was clear.

**A list that has already been concluded cannot be concluded again: "PL-0142 is already verified — it is not waiting for a check"** (also "already final", "already rejected"). WHY: the conclusion of a list at the loading bay is the shipping paperwork refusing to go out, not a second rejection that would mean unpacking a stuffed container.

**A rejected list is closed to new verdicts: "PL-0142 is already rejected — reopen it before checking again".** Reopening is Santosh's or Setumani's, from the packing list, not something bay 5 can do here. WHY: the list has already gone back to Commercial with its findings; changing verdicts underneath them would rewrite the reason it went back.

**A list that is not one of the four dispatch-check states simply does not exist here: "Packing list not found".** A list Commercial is still drafting, or one already shipped, answers that way rather than "you are not allowed to see this". WHY: the second answer would confirm to the bay that the list exists. Same for a line that is not on the list you have open: "Slab not found on this list" / "Cut-to-size line not found on this list".

**There is no Swap button beside a refused cut-to-size piece — only beside a refused slab.** WHY: a slab can be replaced from the shelf; a piece was cut to the customer's size and there is no shelf of replacements. It has to be recut, which is Commercial's work.

**The Swap picker will only offer a like-for-like slab.** It opens saying "Replace #158138 with another Black Galaxy · 2 cm" and "Same design and thickness only. Available slabs, and slabs held for this order." The design and thickness are fixed to the refused slab's and cannot be changed. Each slab offered shows its batch, grade, bay, frame and size with a green "available" or an amber "held · <reference>" tag, and a box at the top narrows the list by slab number or batch. Only the first 150 are shown, and it says so. The button reads "Pick a slab" until one is chosen. If there are none: "No slab of this design and thickness is available or held for this order." A mismatch is named in plain terms — "Slab #158204 cannot replace #158138: 3 cm, not 2 cm". WHY: a swap is a like-for-like the customer never sees on the invoice. A different colour or a 2 cm for a 3 cm is a new order line, not a swap.

**Swapping is refused unless the list has been checked and the slab was actually refused:** "A draft list has no slab to swap — swapping is for a verified or final list whose slab the dispatch check refused", and "Slab #158138 has not been marked unfit — only a refused slab is swapped". WHY: "it looks nicer" is not a refusal, and a list still under the checker's hands is edited the ordinary way.

**Other swap blocks you may see:** "Slab #158204 is already on PL-0142", "Slab #158204 is not in finished goods (or not visible to this login)", and "Nothing was swapped — …" when the stock system would not release the refused slab. WHY: if a swap only half-happened, one slab would be sitting packed against nothing with no screen saying so.

**Downstream, nothing ships until this screen is happy.** When Commercial tries to send the shipment out they get: "Nothing ships until the list is corrected. 2 slab(s) marked unfit by the dispatch check: #158138 (Crack); #158141 (Chipped edge) — swap each one for a slab of the same design and thickness. 1 cut-to-size line(s) not yet checked — the dispatch team has to pass them first." WHY: a packing list cannot be split and a finalised list's contents cannot be edited, so the honest answer is "not this list, not yet", with the lines named.

**Sometimes a rejected slab cannot go back to stock, and it stays on the list rather than vanishing.** You are told on the spot: "1 slab(s) could not be put back and are still on this list: #158138 (could not be read)." The reason written on the line changes too, to something like "Crack — still packed in finished goods: could not be read". WHY: you are standing next to that slab. A slab that quietly disappeared from the list while still sitting in the crate would be unfindable.
gotchas: **Verify and Reject are the same button.** It is green and says "Verify — all fit" while everything passes, and turns red and says "Reject — 3 unfit" the moment anything is marked unfit. People expect two buttons and look for a separate Reject.

**Rejecting is a one-way door from this screen.** The unfit slabs come off the list and go back into stock, the list turns Rejected, and the order is pulled back to Packing for Commercial. Bay 5 cannot undo it or reopen it — only Santosh or Setumani can. Be sure of a finding before you tap it.

**On a Rejected list, Fit and Unfit are greyed — and everything else has gone, not greyed.** There is no Verify button, no note box, no "Mark all as correct", no "Mark crate as correct" and no Swap; they are simply not on the page. Nothing is broken — the check on that list is finished and its findings are already with Commercial. Only "Back to the queue" still works.

**A Verified or Final list looks like it has been locked, but it hasn't — and that is on purpose.** There is no Verify button, but every line still has Fit and Unfit. That is the loading bay: a slab passed last week that turns out cracked as it goes into the container is marked here. Marking it unfit unpacks nothing and moves nothing; it simply stops the shipment until Commercial acts. The screen says so on the spot — "Marked unfit. Nothing ships until Commercial swaps this slab." for a slab, and "Marked unfit. Nothing ships until Commercial recuts this line." for a cut-to-size piece.

**A slab swapped in after the check comes back unchecked, and it is easy to miss.** It shows "Swapped in — not yet checked" in amber, and the band at the top says "1 line(s) still to check — nothing ships until they are marked fit". Until somebody taps Fit on it the truck does not leave, even though the list still reads Verified. The swapped-in row also shows our slab number only — the customer's own number that was printed there is gone with the slab it belonged to.

**The bulk shortcuts only appear while something is unchecked.** Once every line has a verdict, "Mark all as correct" and "Mark crate as correct" disappear from the screen — they have not broken, there is just nothing left for them to mark. They come back at the loading bay too, if a swapped-in line leaves something unchecked.

**A cut-to-size list has zero slabs on it and is still a full job.** The queue used to show a 0 on these and checkers walked past them. The big number now counts slabs and pieces together and the caption reads "cut-to-size lines", so a list of nothing but pieces looks like the work it is.
**The "Something else" reason box has a dead button until you type.** Mark unfit stays greyed while the box is empty; the eight preset reasons work on a single tap with no confirmation step.
**"Mark all as correct" asks for confirmation; "Mark crate as correct" does not.** The crate one fires immediately.
**The queue does not refresh itself.** If a tablet has been sitting on the rack, tap Refresh before trusting the counts.

**Crate headings you did not expect are meaningful, not errors.** "as printed on the cut-to-size sheet" means the customer's drawing sheet uses a crate number we have no crate record for; "A crate that is no longer on this list" means the crate record was removed after those lines went into it. Both are still real boxes on the floor, so they get their own heading rather than being tipped in with loose lines.
**Sizes are shown in whatever unit the order uses**, stated in the header ("sizes in cm"). Do not assume — an export order may be in inches.
**Read the answer after a bulk action, not just the green colour.** "38 marked correct, 2 left unfit" comes back in amber, not green, precisely because the second half is the half that matters.

**A rejected list that comes back is a fresh job, not a half-done one.** When Commercial reopens it, every verdict on it is wiped — the fit ones as well as the unfit ones — because the list is about to change. Expect to walk the whole thing again.
entry.handsTo:
If the list is VERIFIED, it goes straight back to Commercial: the order moves to Ready, and Santosh or Setumani finalise the packing list and get the container loaded. From there Raghav raises the invoice and the delivery challan that travel with it, and Murali handles the freight side. The note you typed is saved onto the list where Commercial reads it.

If the list is REJECTED, the order is pulled back to Packing so it shows up on Commercial's screens as work to do, not as ready to ship. The unfit slabs are returned to stock and come off the list; the good slabs stay packed, because nobody unpacks a good slab. Unfit cut-to-size pieces stay on the list with your reason on them, flagged for Commercial to recut — there is nothing in stock to return a piece cut to a customer's size to. Santosh or Setumani reopen it, repack and send it back through this screen — and reopening clears every verdict on the list, so when it returns it is a whole new check.

If you marked something unfit at the loading bay, Santosh or Setumani pick it up: a slab gets the Swap button (same design and thickness, from available stock or stock already held for this order), and a piece gets recut. Either way the line comes back unchecked on whichever tab the list is already sitting on — Verified or At loading — for the bay to pass, and the shipping paperwork refuses to go out until it does. Every late verdict is also written into the order's history, so Commercial can see why the truck is waiting without anyone having to phone the bay.

entry.title: Invoices — raising, numbering and issuing the commercial invoice
entry.purpose: This is the book of every invoice Pacific has raised against a commercial order — the domestic ones (called DTA, carrying GST) and the export ones (raised under LUT, no GST). The invoice is the document the customer pays against and the paper that travels with the load, so this screen is where the desk checks what a customer is about to be billed, opens the printed copy, and sees at a glance which invoices are still drafts, which are out, and which were cancelled. The invoice itself is not started here: it is drafted from the order, checked and finished on this screen, then issued — and once issued it is fixed.
entry.whoActs: Santosh (manager) does everything, and three things only he or an admin can do: cancel an invoice, move the bank away from the account the proforma named, and retype the exchange rate after an invoice has been issued. Setumani (executive) and Raghav (documents) both write invoices in full — they draft, price, edit and issue — but for them the Cancel button is simply not on the screen, the bank dropdown is greyed with its reason under it, and the rate box locks the moment the invoice is issued. Murali (logistics) is read-only on the invoice screens: he sees the register, opens any invoice, opens any PDF, and every box on the invoice page is greyed with the reason written once across the top; Issue and Cancel do not appear for him there at all. One warning about Murali: on the ORDER's Invoice tab the New invoice and Issue buttons are NOT hidden from him, because that tab goes by what he may do on orders, not on invoices. He can open the form and fill it in, and the refusal only comes when he presses Create draft invoice — "Not available for this login." Nothing is saved; he has simply wasted the typing. The bay 5 dispatch team has no invoice screen whatsoever; if they type the address in they are put back on their Dispatch Check.
steps: Open Invoices from the Commercial menu. Four tiles across the top: how many invoices match, the billed value, how many drafts are on this page, and where you are in the list. The Billed value tile carries a small 'i' — open it and it tells you how the figure is worked out. Below the tiles a filter row: Kind (All, DTA (domestic), Export), Status (All, Draft, Issued, Cancelled), a From and To date, and a Search box that looks at the invoice number, the order number and the client's name. Fifty rows to a page; Previous and Next appear at the bottom only when there is more than one page.

Read a row: the invoice number with its date directly underneath, an FY 26-27 badge on export numbers, then the kind, the order (click through to it), the client, the packing list it was built from, the vehicle and LR, the grand total, the status, and Open to see the printed PDF in a new tab. An amber line under a number saying '2 lines without a rate' means somebody is about to bill slabs at zero.

To raise a new invoice you do not start here — there is no New invoice button on this screen, and the empty register says so. Click the order number, or go to the order and open its Invoice tab. That is where the form lives.

On the order's Invoice tab press New invoice (it becomes Close while the form is open). If the button is not there at all, the order already carries an invoice that has not been cancelled, and the sentence in its place names it. Do not read a visible button as permission: a login that only reads invoices still sees it, and is refused at the end.

Choose the Kind. A domestic order pre-selects DTA — domestic, with GST; an export order pre-selects Export — under LUT, no GST. The hint underneath says which is usual for this order. The choice decides the layout, the tax and which number series the invoice draws from, so change it only if the order itself is filed wrongly. If the order is sold by the group's US company, the DTA choice is greyed out and an amber line says so — that company prints its own invoice, on its own bank, with its own numbers.

Choose whether to draw the lines from a packing list. Left at 'No — use the order's own lines', the invoice bills exactly what the order was priced at. Pick a packing list instead and the lines come from the slabs actually packed — grouped by design and thickness, the quantity summed from the slabs themselves, the rate taken from the order line that matches that design and thickness. Rejected packing lists are not offered.

Check the invoice date. It defaults to today.
