It matters twice: it is what prints, and on a DOMESTIC invoice it decides which year's counter the number is taken from — so backdating a domestic invoice across 1 April takes a number out of last year's run. Export numbers run on one unbroken counter with no year in them, so a date only changes the FY badge beside them.

Leave 'Number (blank takes the next one)' empty unless you are deliberately mirroring a number from elsewhere. Blank means the next number off the counter. An export invoice reads PESPL/N0012 and runs on year after year, which is why the register puts an FY badge beside it; a domestic invoice reads PESPL/N0007/26-27 and starts again each April. A number typed by hand is used exactly as typed and does not move the counter on.

Check 'Issued under GSTIN'. It defaults to Pacific's own registration; the other entry on the list is the group's other registration, Pacific Granites (India) Pvt Ltd. Picking that one on an export invoice pops one amber question — 'Apply this registration to every sheet of the export workbook?' — with three ways out: 'Yes — every sheet', 'No — this invoice only', and 'Keep the current one'. Yes puts it on the packing list, the customer's copy and Annexure C1 as well; No prints it on this invoice only. Escape or 'Keep the current one' is not an answer and leaves the registration where it was. On a domestic invoice the question is never asked — a small grey line says instead that there is no export workbook for it to reach.

Check 'Bank printed'. It arrives already set to the account the order's live proforma named, so the customer pays where his proforma told him to, and a grey line underneath names that proforma. For everyone below Santosh the dropdown is greyed with the reason printed under it.

Fill Vehicle no, Transporter, LR no and E-way bill no if they are known now; all four can be filled later on the invoice itself while it is still a draft. Container no and Seal no are not on this form at all — they come off the packing list where there is one, and are typed on the invoice afterwards.

Check the exchange rate. The box is named for the currency the invoice will actually be raised in — 'Exchange rate (INR per USD)' — and it arrives already carrying the rate typed on the order, so read it rather than assuming it is blank. On any rupee invoice (every domestic one, and an export order priced in rupees) the box is greyed with its reason and the order's rate is dropped rather than copied across. This figure is load-bearing: it is what a payment received in another currency is converted through when the order's advance is tested, and the advance is what lets a truck leave.

Press Create draft invoice (or Cancel to close the form without raising anything). A number is taken, the whole document is frozen — buyer, consignee, notify party, proforma reference, buyer's PO, lines, tax, bank, registration, declaration — and a green line confirms 'Invoice PESPL/N0012 drafted.' From here on, changes to the order do not follow the invoice.

Open the draft from the register or from the row on the order. Along the top: the number with its date and status, Open PDF, a link back to the order, a link to the Export documents on an export invoice, then Issue invoice and, for Santosh, Cancel…

Read the page — it shows exactly what the PDF will print. The Particulars card carries the proforma number and date (labelled PI no & date), the buyer's PO, the sales person, the commodity, the currency, the exchange rate with the day it was typed, the packing list and the time it was issued. Then the Buyer and Consignee blocks, and the Lines table with the running total, the tax and the amount in words underneath.

Price anything amber. A line highlighted in amber carries a quantity and no rate — it came off the packing list for a design the order does not carry. Type into the Rate box and leave Amount blank, and the amount works itself out as quantity times rate; type an amount instead and your figure stands. Press Save rates (Reset rates puts them back), and a green line answers 'Lines saved — the tax and the total were re-derived.'

Fix the registration or the bank on the 'Registration and bank' card if they are wrong, and press Save registration and bank. That button stays grey until you actually change something, and Reset beside it undoes your typing.

Check or set the exchange rate on its own card and press Save rate. It too stays grey until the figure really moves — re-saving 88.4200 over 88.42 changes nothing and is not counted as a change. Every real change stamps the date and both figures go into the order's log. An amber 'no date' means the rate was inherited before the stamp existed — retype it.

Fill the transport boxes on the 'Transport and references' card — Vehicle no, Transporter, LR no, Container no, Seal no, E-way bill no — along with the invoice date and the notes that print under the declaration, and press Save. Reset reloads the card as it was last saved.
Press Open PDF and read the actual document before committing to it.

Press Issue invoice. The invoice is stamped, the order moves forward to Invoiced, the invoice becomes read-only and a green line says 'Invoice PESPL/N0012 issued.' If the button is grey, hover it — the checklist has not been approved yet, and the amber note above the invoice says the same thing.

If an issued invoice turns out to be wrong, Santosh presses Cancel…, types the reason ('Wrong consignee, raised again as PESPL/…') and presses Cancel invoice (or Keep it to back out). The same thing can be done from the order's Invoice tab: Cancel, then the reason box, then Confirm cancel. The number is kept and shown as cancelled; the order may then take a fresh invoice.
refusals: Raising a second invoice on an order is blocked — the New invoice button does not appear and the screen says: 'This order already has invoice PESPL/N0012 (draft). One order carries one invoice — cancel it with a reason before raising another'. One proforma has one invoice: a wrong one is cancelled with a reason on the record and raised again, never doubled up, so nobody can bill the same load twice. Two clerks drafting at the same second are caught the same way — the second one is refused, not given a twin.

Issuing before the checklist is approved is blocked — the Issue invoice button is greyed and both the order's tab and the invoice page say: 'The checklist must be approved before the final invoice — an admin or the Commercial Manager approves it on the order's Overview tab'. Approval is the point at which somebody senior has confirmed the load is what the customer ordered; billing before it means demanding money for goods nobody has signed off. A draft can be fully prepared while you wait.

Editing an issued invoice is blocked: 'Only a draft can be edited (this invoice is issued)'. The customer is already holding that paper — changing it here would leave the ERP and his copy saying different things. The page states the honest repair on the transport card: 'An issued invoice is read-only. Cancel it and raise another if these were wrong.'
Issuing anything that is not a draft is blocked: 'Only a draft can be issued (this invoice is cancelled)'. A number is only ever stamped once.
Issuing an empty invoice is blocked: 'The invoice has no lines — add items to the order and rebuild the draft'. A tax document with no lines is not a document.

Issuing on an order that has been closed off is blocked: 'A cancelled order cannot be invoiced'. This one is only tested when you press Issue, not when you draft — so a draft can quietly exist against an order somebody has since cancelled, and the refusal arrives at the last moment.

Issuing a draft after the selling company on the order has been changed is refused: 'This draft was raised for Monolith Surfaces Inc (USA), but the order now says Pacific Engineered Surfaces Private Limited (India). Cancel it and raise the invoice again, so the number and the printed company come from the same place.' The number was already drawn from one company's series; the paper and the number must belong to the same books.

Changing the bank is blocked for everyone below Santosh — the dropdown is greyed and says: 'The invoice follows the PI's bank; the Commercial Manager may change it'. The proforma already told the customer which account to pay into; moving it afterwards is how payments get lost, so it takes a manager's decision.

Retyping the exchange rate after issue is blocked for Setumani and Raghav: 'The exchange rate on an issued invoice is the Commercial Manager's or an admin's to change'. Once the paper is out, that figure has been seen by the customer and the bank, and it is what a foreign payment is measured against — moving it is the same weight of decision as cancelling the invoice.

The exchange rate on a cancelled invoice is refused to everybody, Santosh included: 'This invoice is cancelled — nothing on it can be changed'. A cancelled document is history and nothing is measured through it any more.

Typing a rate on a rupee invoice is blocked — the box is greyed and says: 'This invoice is priced in rupees, so there is nothing to convert — the rate is rupees per one unit of a foreign currency. Raise the invoice in the currency the money arrives in, or record the receipt in rupees'. A rate means rupees per one dollar; on a rupee invoice it would mean rupees per rupee, convert nothing, and sit on the screen contradicting the receipts card.

A slipped key on the rate is refused: 'The exchange rate must be more than zero', 'The exchange rate must be a number, or blank for no rate', or 'The exchange rate is too large — 4 decimals and at most 8 digits before them'. At zero the advance conversion either divides by nothing or wipes the money out entirely. Blank is allowed and means no rate agreed — and then money arriving in another currency counts toward nothing.

A rate with no date is flagged in amber: 'This rate carries no date. Retype it to stamp it — an undated rate cannot be defended later'. Six months on, a bare figure cannot be explained to an auditor, to the bank, or to a customer asking why his transfer covered 27 per cent and not 30.

Everything on the invoice screens is blocked for Murali, said once across the top rather than as a tooltip on every box: 'This login may read invoices but not change them — ask the Commercial desk'. His desk is enquiries, clients, orders and the freight side; the invoice is Raghav's and Setumani's paper. He still sees every figure, so he can answer a customer's question without being able to alter the bill. The one place he is not warned in advance is the order's Invoice tab, where pressing Create draft invoice or Issue answers 'Not available for this login.'

Cancelling without a reason is blocked: 'Say why the invoice is being cancelled'. The reason goes onto the order's log, because a number that was taken and then killed has to be explainable years later. Cancelling twice is refused with 'This invoice is already cancelled'.

A registration nobody has set up is refused: 'GSTIN 33ABCDE1234F1Z5 is not one the company issues under — add it in Settings first'. A registration number on a tax document has to be one somebody has vouched for, not one typed in a hurry.

A domestic invoice for the group's US company is refused: 'A DTA invoice is an Indian domestic tax document and Monolith Surfaces Inc (USA) does not raise one. This order is marked DOMESTIC and sold by Monolith Surfaces Inc (USA); correct whichever is wrong — the selling company on the order, or its kind — and raise the invoice again.' The screen will not guess which of the two is the mistake, because guessing puts a real document out under the wrong company. On the form itself the DTA choice is simply greyed out for that company, which saves the walk.

Drafting with nothing to bill is refused: 'Nothing to invoice — the order has no line items'. Picking someone else's packing list gets 'That packing list belongs to another order', and a packing list that has since been deleted gets 'Packing list not found'.
A number that already exists is refused: 'Invoice number PESPL/N0012 already exists' — this is what catches a hand-typed number that duplicates one already in the book.

A date typed in some other shape is refused before anything is saved: 'Invoice date must be YYYY-MM-DD'. More generally, a value the screen cannot apply refuses the whole save rather than half of it — 'Could not apply gstin — check the value and try again' names the box that is wrong. Better to be told which box is wrong than to be shown 'Saved' over a change that never landed.

Unpriced lines are warned about rather than blocked, in amber above the invoice: 'Lines 2, 3 have no rate — the order carries no line for that design and thickness. Type the rate before issuing, or the invoice bills those slabs at zero.' It can only happen when the lines come off a packing list, and it is the one mistake on this screen that costs real money.

Two more amber notes warn rather than block. On a domestic invoice: 'The buyer has no GST state code on file, so IGST was assumed. Fill the state code on the client to have CGST + SGST worked out for a Tamil Nadu buyer.' On an export invoice: '2 lines have no design code in the master — the document prints the design name. Codes are added under Settings.' Both let the invoice go out; both mean the paper will read differently from what the desk expects.
gotchas: There is no New invoice button on the Invoices screen. It is always raised from the order's Invoice tab — click the order number in the register to get there. The empty register says so in its message.
A grey Issue invoice button almost always means one thing: the checklist has not been approved yet. Hover it and the reason appears, naming who approves it.

On the invoice screens, Murali's Issue and Cancel buttons are not greyed — they are absent, along with every save button, while the fields themselves grey out. On the order's Invoice tab it is the other way round: New invoice and Issue are fully live for him and only fail when pressed. 'The button was there' is not proof the login may act.
For Setumani and Raghav the Cancel button never appears at all, so 'I can't find Cancel' is not a fault — cancelling is Santosh's or an admin's.

There are FOUR save buttons on one invoice page, each saving only its own card: Save rates on the lines table, Save registration and bank, Save rate on the exchange-rate card, and Save on the transport card. Filling boxes in two cards and pressing one button saves half your work. Two of them (registration and bank, and the rate) stay grey until you have actually changed something, which is the quickest way to tell whether your typing registered.

On the lines table, leaving Amount blank is deliberate — it means the amount is quantity times rate and will re-work itself when you change the rate. Type a figure into Amount and yours stands instead, which is how an odd agreed figure is kept.
Issuing is the point of no return. After it the only field that still moves is the exchange rate, and only for Santosh. Everything else needs a cancellation and a fresh invoice — with a fresh number.

A cancelled invoice keeps its number and stays in the register forever. Numbers are never reused, so the run of numbers can have a gap with an explanation attached rather than a gap nobody can account for.

When Santosh retypes the rate on an already-issued invoice, the PDF the customer holds does not change. The screen then prints an amber line — 'The document prints INR 88.42 per USD; this is the working figure since.' — so nobody quotes the screen at a customer who is reading the paper. The same line appears on the order's Invoice tab.

On a DOMESTIC invoice the date chooses the number's year: dating one 31 March when it is actually April draws the number out of the old year's counter, and that cannot be undone without cancelling. Export numbers have no year in them and come off a single running counter, so the date there only moves the FY badge.

Export numbers run on across years and carry no year, which is why the register shows an FY 26-27 badge beside them. Domestic numbers carry their year already and get no badge. An export order sold by the group's US company takes a third series of its own, reading MSI-1 and so on.

Typing a number by hand into 'Number (blank takes the next one)' does not move the counter on, so the next automatic invoice will still take the number it was going to take. Only use it when mirroring a number from elsewhere.

Drawing lines from a packing list is the only way to end up with an unpriced line: a slab of a design the order does not carry finds no rate to copy. The invoice will go out billing those slabs at zero if nobody types a rate, so the amber warning on the page and the amber note in the register are worth reading every time.

The Billed value tile adds up whatever is on the filter and always prints a rupee sign, even when every invoice on the list is in dollars. It also leaves cancelled invoices out ONLY while no status is chosen — filter to Status: Cancelled and the tile obligingly totals the cancelled ones. Filter by Kind, and read the small 'i', before quoting that figure to anybody.

On an export invoice, a line whose design has no code in the design master prints the design's name instead of a code. The screen flags it — codes are added under Settings, which is an admin screen, so it needs the admin login.

Picking the other registration asks its one question only on an export invoice, and only at the moment you pick it. Closing the question with Escape or 'Keep the current one' is not an answer — it leaves the registration where it was. Switching the form to DTA while the question is open closes it the same way.

Container no and Seal no are not on the new-invoice form. They arrive from the packing list when one is named, and can only be typed afterwards on the invoice's transport card — worth knowing before an export document set is built on them.

The exchange-rate box on the new-invoice form is not empty: it starts with whatever rate the order carries. On a rupee invoice that inherited figure is thrown away rather than carried over, which is the right answer but not an obvious one.
entry.handsTo: Pressing Issue moves the order forward to Invoiced (an order already further along is not dragged back) and locks the invoice. The printed PDF becomes the customer's copy — Raghav sends it and files it. On an export order the same frozen invoice is what the Export documents set is built from, so the packing list, the customer's copy and Annexure C1 take their figures, registration and bank from this invoice; if either the registration or the bank is wrong, it can only be corrected here, and only while the invoice is still a draft. That is Raghav's next screen. The goods still do not move on the invoice alone: the truck is held until the advance has actually been received against the order — 'The advance has not been received: the truck does not leave before it' — and on a foreign order it is the working exchange rate on this invoice that decides whether a payment in dollars counts as enough. Murali and the bay 5 team pick it up from there with the dispatch check and the delivery challans; Santosh is the one who waives the advance or cancels the invoice if something has to be redone.

entry.title: Delivery challans
entry.purpose: This is the book for goods that move without being sold — samples, display slabs, stands going to a showroom, material to the sister company. It produces the four-copy delivery challan that travels with the lorry: one copy for the buyer, one for the transporter, one for Central Excise and one for us. It also sits alongside a domestic invoice when goods move under an order. The values printed on it are declared approximate values, not revenue, and the page says so itself: every copy carries the line "Amount Declared is approximate value of the goods".
entry.whoActs: Nobody on the commercial desk is read-only here. Santosh, Setumani, Raghav and Murali can all raise a draft, edit it, save it, issue it and print it — this screen is one of the few where all four write. The one thing split off is cancelling: only Santosh (or an admin) can cancel a challan, and for the other three the "Cancel…" button is simply not on the page rather than greyed out, so do not hunt for it. Bay 5 cannot reach this screen at all — if a dispatch login types the address it is sent straight back to the Dispatch Check. Once a challan is issued or cancelled, every field turns grey for everyone, Santosh included, and the Save, Reset, "Add a line" and "Remove" buttons disappear altogether; the panel is then headed "What this challan says" instead of "Edit this draft". That is the document being finished, not a permission problem.
steps: Open Delivery Challans from the side menu. The book lists every challan, newest challan date first, fifty to a page, with the date printed directly under each number.

Read the four boxes across the top: how many challans match what you are looking at, their total declared value, how many rows on this page are still drafts, and where you are in the pages. The small "i" circle beside Declared value opens a note explaining what that sum is and why it is not revenue.

Narrow the book with the four controls: Status (All, Draft, Issued, Cancelled), a From date, a To date, and a Search box that matches the challan number, the consignee name or the PO reference. Changing any of them puts you back on page one. Previous and Next sit at the bottom when there is more than one page. When nothing matches you get "No challan matches this filter."

On any row, click the challan number to open it, or click Open in the PDF column to go straight to print. The Order column links back to that order's Invoice tab when the challan was raised against an order.

To raise one, press New challan, on the right of the filter row. If it belongs to an order, go to that order's Invoice tab instead and press "New challan for this order" — that ties the two together for you and saves you finding the order by hand.
On the new-challan form, fill the top row: Challan date (already today), "PO no & date" (already says Verbal), Commodity (already says Artificial Quartz Slabs) and Lorry no.

Name the consignee. There are two boxes: a search of the client master, and a Consignee name you can type into. Picking a client from the search fills the name box only — the address and GSTIN boxes stay empty on screen, and the client's own address and GSTIN are pulled in when you save, but only into boxes you left blank. For a showroom that is not a customer yet, leave the search alone and type the name, the address and the GSTIN yourself. Type the address one line per printed line.

Fill the lines: material description, quantity, unit (Nos, Box, SQFT or Set), SQFT, rate, Amount (approx) and HSN. "Add a line" gives you another row; "Remove" takes one away, and is not offered on the last remaining row. Leave Amount blank and it works itself out — rate times SQFT when the line has an area, rate times quantity otherwise. The total SQFT, the grand total and the amount in words update under the table as you type.

Write the Purpose if this movement needs a particular note on the printed page. Leave it blank and the standard note prints: "Note: Please note that these items are for display purposes only and not for sale". Either way a second line prints under it saying the amount declared is approximate. Internal notes print small under the declaration on all four copies, so keep them fit for an outsider to read.
Leave "Challan number" blank so the challan takes the next number in the book. Type one only when you are copying a number that was already issued somewhere else.

Press "Create draft challan". It saves as a draft, takes its number, and opens the challan's own page. "Cancel" on this form just abandons the typing and returns you to the book — it does not cancel anything.

On the challan's own page, check the Summary panel (consignee, GSTIN, PO ref, lorry number, declared value, and the issue time once it has one, with the amount in words underneath) and the Copies printed panel, which lists the four copies that will come out of the printer. If the challan belongs to an order, an Order button beside the print button takes you to that order's Invoice tab.

While it is still a draft, correct anything except the number: edit the fields and press Save. A green "Saved." confirms it. Reset reloads the saved version and throws away whatever you have typed since, with no warning.
Press "Issue challan" when it is right. The badge turns green, the time is stamped, a green line says the challan is issued, and the whole form goes grey.

Press "Open PDF (4 copies)" and print. Four A4 pages come out, each labelled top right — Original Buyer Copy, Duplicate Transporter Copy, Triplicate Central Excise Copy, Quadruplicate Assessee Copy. Hand the driver his copy, keep ours.

If a challan turns out to be wrong, Santosh presses "Cancel…", types the reason and presses "Cancel challan" ("Keep it" backs out). This works on a draft as well as an issued one. The challan stays in the book showing CANCELLED, with a line at the top saying its number is kept so the book accounts for it, and the reason written into its notes. Raise a fresh one — a wrong challan is never corrected after issue.
refusals: Creating a challan with no filled-in lines is refused: "Add at least one line to the challan". A challan is the paper that says what left the yard; a page that lists nothing proves nothing and is no use to a check post.

Creating or saving without a consignee is refused: "Name the consignee". The transporter and the check post read that one line to know where the goods are going, so the challan cannot exist without it. Picking a client from the master counts as naming one.

Pressing Issue on a challan with no lines is refused: "The challan has no lines — add at least one before issuing". This is reachable, because a draft whose lines you have blanked out CAN be saved — only issuing is stopped. Once issued nothing can be added, so the emptiness would be permanent.

Pressing Issue on something already issued or cancelled is refused: "Only a draft can be issued (this challan is issued)". It stops one movement being stamped twice and two sets of copies circulating on one number.

Editing an issued challan is refused: "Only a draft can be edited (this challan is issued)". The Save button is gone by then, so you normally see this only when somebody else issued the challan while you had it open. Copies are already with the driver and with Central Excise; the paper in their hands and our record have to say the same thing, so the only way back is to cancel and raise another.

Typing a challan number that already exists is refused: "Challan number … already exists", naming the number you typed. Two movements sharing one number makes the book impossible to audit, which is the whole point of a numbered document.

Cancelling without typing a reason is refused: "Say why the challan is being cancelled." A cancelled number stays in the book forever and somebody reading it in a year has to be able to see why the goods did not go.
Cancelling something already cancelled is refused: "This challan is already cancelled".

Typing an order reference that does not exist is refused: "Order not found", and picking a consignee whose client record has since gone is refused: "Consignee client not found". A challan pointing at nothing would drop out of the order's history.

Emptying the Challan date box on a saved challan leaves the date as it was; on a new challan it falls back to today in India. There is a refusal behind it — "Challan date must be YYYY-MM-DD" — but the box is a date picker, so in normal use you will not meet it.

Opening this screen with a login that does not have it lands you on a page saying your login is not allowed to open it — nothing went wrong and nothing was lost. The messages "Not available for this login." and "Please sign in." appear in a red strip on the screen itself when something is refused while you are already on it, most often because the session timed out with the book left open; sign in again and the work you had typed but not saved is gone. A bay 5 dispatch login that reaches for the challan book is sent to its Dispatch Check instead, because that is the one screen it has.
gotchas: The number is taken the moment you press "Create draft challan", not when you issue it. Abandoning a draft still uses that number up, and the next challan gets the one after. A refused attempt does not eat a number — the consignee and the lines are checked first. Nothing is ever deleted, only cancelled, so the book accounts for every number.

A number you type in by hand does not move the counter on. That is deliberate — it lets you mirror a number issued in Tally without eating an ERP number — but it means two people typing numbers by hand can collide, and only the duplicate refusal catches it. The greyed example in the box is an old challan number; the ones the counter gives out look like PESPL/DC/N0021/26.
The challan number cannot be changed after the draft exists. The number box only appears on the new-challan form; on the challan's own page it is gone, even while the challan is still a draft.

Picking a client does not visibly fill anything but the name. The address and the GSTIN stay blank on screen and are taken from the client record only when you save, and only if you left them blank — so what you see before saving is not what will print. If you type over the name, address or GSTIN, what you typed wins. The Clear button beside the search clears the consignee name along with the client. On a challan you reopen, the search box is blank even though a client is attached; the Clear button showing is how you know one is.

"Order id (optional)" wants the system's own private reference for the order — a long string of letters and numbers — not the order number you would say out loud. Typing an order number there gives "Order not found". Raise the challan from the order's Invoice tab instead and it is filled in for you.

A line with no description, no quantity, no rate and no SQFT is silently dropped when you save. The form starts with two blank rows, so a challan you thought had two lines can come back with one — and a draft can end up with no lines at all, which only shows up when you try to issue it.
Typing 0 in the Amount box counts as leaving it blank — the amount is worked out from the rate instead. A genuinely free line has to have a zero rate, not a zero amount.

A draft prints. "Open PDF" works at any status, so an unissued challan can reach the printer by mistake — it comes out stamped "DRAFT — not issued" in orange under the title, and a cancelled one stamped "CANCELLED" in red. Look for those stamps before handing anything to a driver.

Internal notes are not internal to the paper: they print small under the declaration on all four copies. The cancellation reason is added to those same notes, so a cancelled challan reprinted later carries the reason on its face.

The Declared value box is not revenue and not a sales figure. It is the approximate declared value of the goods on the move, and it says "cancelled excluded" — but that caption only holds while you are not filtering by status. Set Status to Cancelled and the box obediently totals the cancelled challans while still claiming to exclude them.

The date box starts at today on the clock of the machine you are on. If it is cleared, a new challan is dated today in India, not the UTC day — which matters for a challan raised before 5:30 in the morning, and especially on 1 April, when the wrong day would pull the number from last financial year's counter.
The bank block printed on the challan is always the export bank (Kotak), whatever the movement is. It comes from Settings, which only an admin can change.

The consignee address prints one line per line you typed. If you type it all on one line it is split at the commas instead, which is usually close enough but not always — and an address pulled from a client record arrives as one comma-separated line, so it prints split that way.
Search in the book covers the number, the consignee name and the PO reference only. It does not find a challan by its lorry number, even though the lorry column is right there.

Nothing anywhere in the system forces a challan to exist before a lorry leaves. The dispatch check does not look for one. Whether a movement needs a challan is a judgement the desk makes, not something the screen will remind you about.

Editing a draft redoes every line's amount, the grand total and the amount in words from scratch, so the screen and the printed page can never disagree. The words include the paise — 48,708.75 is worded down to the seventy-five paise, because the page prints two decimals in four copies and one of them goes to Central Excise.
entry.handsTo: The four printed copies leave with the lorry: the driver carries the Transporter copy, the buyer gets the Original, the Central Excise copy goes with the consignment paperwork and the Assessee copy stays with us. Back in the system, a challan raised against an order writes itself into that order's history — drafted, edited, issued, or cancelled with the reason — and shows up on the order's Invoice tab beside the invoices, which is where Raghav and Santosh look when they are reconciling what went out against what was billed. The challan itself ends here; there is no further stage and nothing downstream waits on it.

entry.title: Design codes and colours (the design master, and the customer article list beside it)
entry.purpose: This is the master list of our designs: one row per design carrying the owner's item code that goes on order lines and export documents, the shade the plant sequences production by, and the colour read off a physical sample with the hand-held meter. A link at the top leads to a second screen that belongs to the same desk, "Customer articles and labels" — the customer's own article codes, descriptions and thirteen-digit barcodes, one row per design AND size, which is what the crate, piece and edge labels print from.
entry.whoActs:
Santosh (Commercial Manager) and any admin login are the only people who can change anything on either screen — design codes, shades, colours, the customer's item codes, barcodes, and each customer's barcode series.

Setumani (Executive) and Murali (Logistics) both get the "Design codes" row in the Commercial sidebar, can open both screens, search them and read every code and colour, but every control that writes is greyed. The design master carries a grey banner at the top: "Read-only for this login. Codes, shades and colours are changed by the Commercial Manager or an admin." The article list carries its own: "Read-only for this login. Item codes and barcodes are changed by the Commercial Manager or an admin."

Not every greyed control explains itself, so do not go looking for a tip that is not there. On the design master only "Seed from stock" repeats that sentence when you hover it — the code box, the notes box, the shade drop-down, the Confirmed tick and Add are simply grey with nothing on hover. On the article list every greyed button (New article, Generate, Edit, Delete, Save series) does repeat "Item codes and barcodes are changed by the Commercial Manager or an admin." on hover, and the New article form does not open at all for a read-only login rather than opening greyed.

Two things a read-only login CAN still do, both deliberate. First, the colour window still OPENS for them, because looking a design's reading up is most of what the screen is for; inside it only Save colour and Clear colour are greyed, under their own grey banner: "Read-only for this login — the colour is the Commercial Manager's or an admin's to set." Second, and more useful day to day: the labels panel at the bottom of the article list is NOT read-only. Setumani and Murali pick a packing list and print crate, piece and edge labels exactly as Santosh does. Printing a label is not changing the master.

Raghav (Documents) does not have either screen — no sidebar row, and typing the address lands him on "You do not have access to that page": "Your login is not allowed to open /office/commercial/design-codes. Nothing went wrong and nothing was lost — the page simply is not part of what this account can see." The bay 5 dispatch team has only the Dispatch Check and never reaches this.
steps: Open Design codes from the Commercial sidebar. The list loads with one row per design and a running count above it: so many designs, so many shades still unconfirmed, so many without a code, so many without a colour.

Find a design by typing in the Find box — it filters as you type and matches the design name, our item code or the colour name. Two tick-boxes narrow it further: "Unconfirmed shades only" and "No colour yet". All three work for read-only logins too.

Press "Seed from stock" to pull in every design finished goods knows about that has no row here yet, whatever the stock status. Each new row arrives with a shade guessed from its name, marked unconfirmed, and with no colour at all. It is safe to press twice — the second time it says "Every design in stock already has a row."
Type the owner's item code into the Code box on a row (it shows in capitals, e.g. VGWT10301A). It saves the moment you click away or press Enter. There is no Save button — each box saves itself.
Pick the shade — light, medium or dark — from the drop-down on the row. Choosing one also ticks Confirmed for you in the same action. Setting it back to "— none —" unticks it.

Or tick Confirmed by hand once somebody has actually looked at the design. Until that is ticked the chip under the design name carries a question mark — "medium?", "light?", "dark?" — and the design counts as a guess.
Click the colour button on the row (a small swatch square, then the colour name with the L* reading under it) to open the colour window for that design.

In the colour window, type the colour name and the L*, a* and b* readings off the sample. Each box shows the range it accepts underneath. The big square swatch redraws itself from those three numbers as you type.

If you would rather fix the colour by eye, type a hex like #F2EFE9 into the "Hex (overrules the reading)" box. The three readings are immediately worked backwards from it and rewritten, because L* is what the production queue reads. A grey line tells you which one is deciding, and a "Use #XXXXXX" button puts you back on the measured one.

Press "Save colour". All five fields save together — this is the one place on the screen that saves as a set rather than field by field. "Clear colour" empties all five and the design falls back to its shade word; it is greyed on a design that has no colour to clear.
Type anything worth remembering into the Notes box on the row ("Owner's list, Sept"). It saves on leaving the box. The last column shows the date the row was last changed.

To add a design that stock does not know yet, type it into "Add a design by hand" at the bottom, exactly as stock spells it, and press Add. It arrives with a guessed, unconfirmed shade and no colour, like a seeded one.
For the customer's own codes and barcodes, follow the link in the header to the customer article list.

On the article list, search with the Find box and press Search (or Enter) — unlike the design master, typing alone changes nothing until you do. A Clear button appears once a search is running. The Customer drop-down offers "Every customer", "Ours (no customer)" and each customer by name.

Pick one named customer in that drop-down and their barcode series card appears, showing their company prefix, the floor the series starts from, how many digits the item reference gets and its range, the highest reference actually in use, the number of articles on file and how many have no barcode, and — most usefully — the exact next code it would hand out, so you can check it by eye against their sheet before printing anything.

To set that series up, type the company prefix, the "Next item reference (floor)" and a note on the card and press "Save series". The prefix is judged as you type and the verdict shows under the card.

Press "New article" and fill in: customer (or leave it as "Ours"), design, length, width and thickness in centimetres, the barcode, the item code, the description and any notes. Press "Add article" to store it, or Cancel to drop it. The barcode is judged as you type — a green line reads "8720847172228 is a valid EAN-13.", a red one says exactly what is wrong, and leaving it blank gives "No barcode: crates of this article print the item code and the size, with no bars."
Press Edit on any row to reopen that article in the same form; the button then reads "Save changes".

Press "Generate" on a single row that has no barcode — the button only appears on rows without one — or "Generate for N blank article(s)" on the series card to fill every blank article this customer has in one run. The bulk run asks first: "Generate a barcode for every article of Desert Stone Ltd that has none — 14 of them? Codes the customer sent are left alone."
Press Delete on a row to remove an article. It asks first, and says what it costs.
The table shows 50 articles at a time, with Previous and Next and "Page 2 of 7" between them.

Scroll to "Labels off a packing list", pick a packing list, and read the warnings before printing — which lines have no article on file, which have an article but no usable barcode, and which pieces are too thin for an edge label. The table below shows exactly what each crate label will print and which crates will go out with no bars. Then press "Crate labels (PDF)", "Piece labels (PDF)" or "Edge labels (PDF)"; each opens in a new tab. The lines under the table say how many piece labels that is, how many A4 sheets, and how big the edge label works out in millimetres.
refusals: Setumani and Murali cannot change anything, on either screen. The banner reads "Read-only for this login. Codes, shades and colours are changed by the Commercial Manager or an admin." (on the article list, "Item codes and barcodes are changed by the Commercial Manager or an admin."). The controls are greyed, never hidden, so nobody wonders whether a button exists. The reason: one person owns the master, or two desks end up typing two different codes for the same design and the export paperwork stops agreeing with itself.

Raghav and the bay 5 team cannot open either screen at all. Typing the address gives "You do not have access to that page" and "Your login is not allowed to open /office/commercial/design-codes. Nothing went wrong and nothing was lost — the page simply is not part of what this account can see." The reason: this list is nobody's job on their desks, and a screen shown with everything greyed is worse than no screen.
The Confirmed tick-box is greyed while a row has no shade chosen. The reason: "confirmed" is a statement about a shade, and there is nothing to confirm until one is picked.

An item code already on another design is refused: "Code VGWT10301A is already Carrara Royale's." The reason: that code is what the customer's paperwork identifies a design by, so two designs under one code makes an export line ambiguous at their end.

A shade that is not one of the three is refused: "Shade must be one of LIGHT, MEDIUM, DARK". The reason: an empty shade column means "nobody has guessed yet", and the production queue would silently treat it as medium — a claim nobody made.

A hex that is half-typed or mistyped refuses the save, with the box outlined red and Save colour greyed: "The hex must read like #F2EFE9". The reason: the screen must never save a colour different from the swatch it is showing you.

A reading outside its axis is refused: "L* must be between 0 and 100", "a* must be between -128 and 127". The reason: a stored 300 would draw a black swatch and make the plant clean as if the design were dark.

A barcode with a wrong digit is refused as you type it, naming the digit: "The check digit should be 8, not 3 — 8720847172228 is the code these twelve digits make." Twelve digits pasted off a sheet gets "A barcode is thirteen digits and this one has twelve — the missing check digit is 8, so the full code is 8720847172228." Anything with a letter or a stray character in it gets "A barcode is thirteen digits — "8720847ABC28" is not one of them." While any of those is showing, the Add article / Save changes button is greyed. The reason: a code refused here costs a retype; the same code refused at the customer's gate costs the container.

A barcode already on another article is refused outright: "8720847172266 is on both 220x19.5x2 and 220x15x2. One of them has to give it up before any barcode for this client is generated or printed." A second button then appears under the message — "Store it without the barcode" — so the row is not lost. The reason: one barcode belongs to one article and to nothing else, and a reused code scans as the wrong goods.

While any one of a customer's articles carries that sentence, none of that customer's barcodes are generated and the Crate and Edge label buttons are dead with the reason on hover: "This customer's barcodes are stopped until a duplicate is settled." followed by the colliding pair. Piece labels still print, because they carry no barcode to be wrong. The reason: printing forty crates while two articles argue over one code sends the argument to the customer's yard.

The same customer, design and size twice is refused: "Desert Silk 101x19.5x2 is already on the list as CQBE 101x19.5x2 — edit that row rather than adding a second one." The reason: those three things are the article's identity; a second row means two codes for one thing.

Generate is greyed on an "Ours" row: "An article of ours has no GS1 prefix to generate from — the series belongs to a customer." The reason: a code invented under nobody's prefix is not a barcode, just thirteen digits that will one day collide with somebody's real article.

Generate is greyed when the customer has no prefix on file — "There is no GS1 prefix on file to generate from." — and the card says "This client has no GS1 company prefix on file, so there is no series to allocate a barcode from." The reason: a generated code must continue the customer's own series, and there is nothing to continue.

The bulk Generate is also greyed when there is nothing left to do: "Every article of this customer already has a barcode." Asking for one anyway on rows that all have codes answers "Every article picked already has a barcode, so there is nothing to generate."

Generate never overwrites a code the customer sent. Those rows are skipped and listed under the card: "CQBE 101x19.5x2 already carries 8720847172228, which came off the customer's own file — their codes are never overwritten." A code we generated ourselves is skipped too, more briefly. The reason: their codes are already printed on stock in their warehouse, and ours are already on a label somewhere.

A malformed company prefix is refused with the arithmetic: "A GS1 company prefix is 6 to 11 digits and this one has 5 — the item reference takes the rest of the twelve." The reason: how many digits the prefix takes decides how many are left for the item reference, and guessing wrong produces thirteen digits that are not the customer's code at all.

A bad floor is refused: "The next item reference is a whole number, zero or more — it is the floor the series starts from, not a code." And if the series is exhausted: "The item references under GS1 prefix 8720847 run from 00000 to 99999 and the series has reached the end, so there is no next code to give — this client needs a second company prefix from GS1."

If somebody types one of the same codes in while a bulk run is being prepared, nothing at all is written: "One of these codes was taken while this run was being prepared, so nothing was allocated. Try again — the next run goes above whatever was just entered." The reason: half a run of barcodes is worse than none.

An incomplete article is refused by field: "Which design is this article? The design is half of its key.", "Give the length in centimetres — it is part of the article's key.", "The length has to be more than zero centimetres." The reason: these forms are filled off a customer's spreadsheet with a dozen rows on it, and "invalid" would mean re-reading all twelve.
All three label buttons are dead until a packing list is chosen, with "Pick a packing list first." on hover.

An edge label is refused on a piece too thin to carry one, and the line is listed instead of printed: "A 12 mm edge leaves 3.2 mm for the bars once the label's clearance, margins and digits are taken off, and under 6 mm of bars an EAN-13 scans as nothing — print this one's barcode on the crate label instead of the edge." The reason: a sticker whose bars are too short does not scan at all, and a roll of them looks perfectly fine coming off the printer.
gotchas: There is no Save button on the design master and no Cancel. Every box saves itself the moment you click away or press Enter, one field at a time. That is deliberate — the owner's code list arrives design by design, and a Save-all across 160 rows would lose an afternoon's typing to one bad code. The colour window is the only exception: its five fields are one reading off one sample and save together, and a refused save leaves the window open with your numbers still in it.
Choosing a shade from the drop-down silently ticks Confirmed as well. Setting it back to "— none —" unticks it. If you only meant to try a shade on for size, it is now recorded as confirmed.

Saving a colour, a hex or a shade quietly changes the plant's schedule. The green line after the save says so — "Cleaning hours re-derived on 4 queued request(s)." — and may add a warning like "Alabaster Noir L* 12 → Super White L* 92 — 6 h of cleaning instead of 3". A design turning out darker than its name suggested is exactly the case this exists for, so read that line rather than dismissing it. Nobody on the commercial desk can open the production queue itself, so that green line is the only sight you get of what your save just did.

Nothing on this screen removes a design. There is no Delete button on any row and no bulk clear — the only things you can do to a row are edit it or add a new one. If a master row ever does disappear, every queued request for that design falls back to medium and its cleaning hours move with it.

"Seed from stock" never touches a row somebody has already edited, and never invents a colour. The shade it writes is only a guess off the name — "white", "bianco", "carrara", "calacatta", "ivory", "cream", "statuario" read light; "black", "nero", "grey", "charcoal", "dark", "brown", "graphite" read dark; a name with both or neither lands on medium — and it wears a "?" until somebody confirms it.

The design name is the key, and capitals genuinely do not matter anywhere: typing CARRARA ROYALE finds and saves onto the row stored as Carrara Royale, and the seed will not make a second row for a stock name that differs only in case. Spaces at either end are trimmed for you. A different SPELLING is the real risk — that does make a second master row, with its own code and its own shade.

The chip under the design name is the quickest read on the row: the word plus a "?" while the shade is only a guess, a dot of the real colour once one is on file, and hovering it gives the colour name, the hex, the L* and "shade guessed from the name — not confirmed". Only a medium chip is amber; light reads pale and dark reads dark, so an unconfirmed light design is easy to skim past.

In the colour window the hex and the readings chase each other. Typing a hex rewrites L*, a* and b*; editing any of L*, a* or b* rewrites the hex. That is on purpose — a stale hex left sitting beside new numbers is how the wrong colour gets saved — but it means you cannot type a hex and then "correct" one of the readings without losing the hex.

Read-only logins can open the colour window and read everything inside it, and they can print every label at the bottom of the article list. Only Save colour, Clear colour and the controls that change a code or a barcode are greyed. This is not a bug.

The customer article list is a different shape from the design master: one row per design AND size. Twelve rows for one design is normal, and two customers may sell the same design at the same size under different codes without either being wrong.

Every code in the table is tagged "customer" or "ours" beside it. That tag is not decoration — it is what decides whether a code can ever be replaced, and it is why a bulk generate skips some rows and fills others.

The barcode series card only appears after you pick one named customer in the filter. "Ours (no customer)" has no series at all. There is no "the GS1 prefix" in general — each customer has their own, and the next customer's may be a different length with less room left for the item reference.

Generating never fills a gap in a series. The owner's file skips 17227 and the system will not reuse it, because a gap is far more likely to be a code already printed on stock that shipped than a free slot. All a skipped number costs is a number.

Changing a customer's company prefix leaves every code already issued exactly as it is, and says so: "3 article(s) of this customer carry codes under a different prefix. They are left exactly as they are, and the series continues under 8720847 alone." A prefix is changed because GS1 issued a second one, not to correct history.

Deleting an article does not stop the design being packed — its crates simply print with no bars. The confirmation says it plainly: "Delete Desert Silk 101x19.5x2? Crates of it will then print with no barcode."

A duplicate block survives an ordinary edit. Fixing the notes or the description does not clear it. Only two things do: giving that row a code of its own, or ticking "This duplicate is settled — clear it and let this customer's barcodes print again", which is somebody stating that the customer has said whose code it is.

The labels panel gives THREE warning lists and they look alike. One names lines with no article on file — somebody here types those in. One names lines that have an article but no usable barcode — either the customer has not sent it, or a digit on file is wrong, and it tells you which. The third names pieces too thin for an edge label, which is nobody's mistake. The first two both print a crate label without bars; the third only affects the edge run.

Edge labels print deliberately short bars. A 2 cm slab edge leaves about 13.4 mm of bars, 59% of the standard height, and the panel says so in millimetres under the table. It is a chosen trade-off — the operator has to hold the scanner straighter, the code still reads — not a printing fault.
The article list shows 50 rows at a time and any new search or change of customer jumps back to page 1. An empty table after a search usually means no such article, not an empty page.
entry.handsTo: Three places pick this up. The shade and the L* reading go to the production queue, where they decide how many hours the plant spends cleaning between one design and the next — a dark design followed by a light one costs the abrupt figure instead of the ordinary one, and any change made here re-derives that on every request already queued. Nobody on the commercial desk, Santosh included, can open that queue, so the green line after a save is the whole of what you will ever see of it — read it. The design's item code goes onto order lines and the export documents Raghav prepares. The customer's article rows feed the crate, piece and edge labels printed off a packing list, which the packers stick on crates and pieces in bay 5, and the barcode on them is what gets scanned at the customer's gate a fortnight later — which is why a code refused on this screen is cheap and the same code refused there is not.
